# 12-Week Home Strength Programme
### Client Profile: 27-Year-Old Male Beginner | Equipment: Yoga Mat + Doorway Pull-Up Bar

---

## Programme Philosophy

This programme is built around a fundamental truth: a beginner's body responds powerfully to almost any progressive overload stimulus, which means the limiting factor is not equipment — it is consistency and intelligent progression. Using bodyweight as the primary resistance tool, we will exploit tempo manipulation, leverage changes, unilateral loading, and volume progression to drive genuine strength adaptation across all three phases. The pull-up bar expands the programme significantly, allowing true vertical pulling and hanging work that most mat-only programmes cannot access.

The programme runs across **three four-week phases**, each with a distinct training emphasis. Sessions are written as **three days per week** with a minimum of one rest day between sessions, giving the client flexibility to fit training around his schedule. Each session runs approximately **45–60 minutes**.

---

## Movement Foundations

Before diving into the weekly structure, it is worth naming the six movement patterns this programme trains consistently throughout all twelve weeks. Every session will touch most of these patterns, and progression within each pattern is the primary driver of strength development.

- **Horizontal Push** — press-up variations
- **Horizontal Pull** — inverted row variations (using the pull-up bar low in a doorframe or a sturdy table edge)
- **Vertical Pull** — pull-up and chin-up progressions
- **Squat** — bilateral and unilateral squat patterns
- **Hip Hinge** — glute bridge, single-leg hinge, and Nordic curl progressions
- **Core/Anti-Rotation** — plank, hollow body, and rotational control work

---

## Phase 1 — Weeks 1–4: Foundation and Motor Learning

**Goal:** Establish movement quality, build connective tissue resilience, develop body awareness, and introduce the client to training stress without overwhelming recovery capacity.

**Training Structure:** Full-body sessions, three days per week. Sets are kept moderate, rest periods are generous, and tempo is used deliberately to slow movements down and build control. The client should finish each session feeling worked but not destroyed.

**Key Tempo Note:** Exercises in this phase use a **3-1-1 tempo** — three seconds on the lowering phase, one second pause at the bottom, one second on the lifting phase. This is non-negotiable in Phase 1. It builds body awareness, eliminates momentum, and creates genuine time under tension even with bodyweight loads.

---

### Week 1

**Session A**

Begin each session with a five-minute general warm-up: thirty seconds of jumping jacks, thirty seconds of hip circles each direction, thirty seconds of arm circles, thirty seconds of cat-cow on the mat, and thirty seconds of bodyweight squats performed slowly. This sequence repeats twice.

- **Incline Press-Up** (hands on a windowsill or sturdy chair) — 3 sets of 10 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Dead Hang** (from pull-up bar, overhand grip) — 3 sets of 20 seconds, 90 seconds rest
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Plank** — 3 sets of 20 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- **Scapular Pull-Up** (hanging from bar, depress and retract shoulder blades without bending elbows) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 90 seconds rest

Finish with five minutes of static stretching: hip flexors, chest, lats, and hamstrings, holding each position for thirty seconds.

**Session B**

Warm-up as above.

- **Incline Press-Up** — 3 sets of 10 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Inverted Row** (bar set low in doorframe, body at roughly 45-degree angle, heels on floor) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets of 8 reps each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 10 reps each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets of 6 reps each side, controlled, 60 seconds rest
- **Dead Hang** — 3 sets of 25 seconds, 90 seconds rest

Finish with the same stretching protocol.

**Session C**

Warm-up as above.

- **Incline Press-Up** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 10 reps, 90 seconds rest
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Side Plank** — 3 sets of 15 seconds each side, 60 seconds rest
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 8 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest

Finish with stretching.

---

### Week 2

The structure mirrors Week 1 but volume increases slightly. The client should be finding the incline press-up and bodyweight squat more manageable now. If he can complete all sets with clean form and the prescribed tempo, progress as follows.

**Session A**

- **Incline Press-Up** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Dead Hang** — 3 sets of 30 seconds
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Plank** — 3 sets of 25 seconds
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 10 reps

**Session B**

- **Incline Press-Up** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 10 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets of 10 reps each leg, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 12 reps each leg, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets of 8 reps each side
- **Dead Hang** — 3 sets of 30 seconds

**Session C**

- **Floor Press-Up** (standard press-up — introduce this now if the incline version feels controlled) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, or continue incline at 3 sets of 15 if floor press-up form breaks down
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 12 reps
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 12 reps each leg
- **Side Plank** — 3 sets of 20 seconds each side
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 10 reps, 3-1-1 tempo

---

### Week 3

This week introduces the first genuine progression in exercise difficulty. The client moves to floor-level press-ups if he has not already, and we introduce the first assisted pull-up attempt.

**Session A**

- **Press-Up** (floor level) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- **Negative Pull-Up** (jump or step to top position, lower over 5 seconds, step down, repeat) — 3 sets of 3 reps, 2 minutes rest
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 2-0-1 tempo (slightly faster now)
- **Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 15 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Hollow Body Hold** — 3 sets of 15 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 12 reps

**Session B**

- **Press-Up** — 3 sets of 8 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets of 12 reps each leg
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 15 reps each leg
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets of 10 reps each side
- **Negative Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 3 reps, 2 minutes rest

**Session C**

- **Press-Up** — 3 sets of 10 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 3-1-1 tempo
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 3 sets of 20 reps
- **Glute Bridge** — 3 sets of 20 reps
- **Side Plank** — 3 sets of 25 seconds each side
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 3 sets of 15 reps

---

### Week 4 — Deload

Week 4 is a deliberate deload. Volume drops by approximately 40%, intensity stays the same, and the client performs only two sessions this week rather than three. This is not optional. Beginners often feel they do not need deloads, but connective tissue adaptation lags behind muscular adaptation, and this week protects the joints and tendons while consolidating the neural patterns built in weeks one through three.

**Session A (Deload)**

- **Press-Up** — 2 sets of 8 reps, controlled tempo
- **Negative Pull-Up** — 2 sets of 3 reps
- **Bodyweight Squat** — 2 sets of 12 reps
- **Glute Bridge** — 2 sets of 12 reps
- **Plank** — 2 sets of 20 seconds
- **Inverted Row** — 2 sets of 8 reps

**Session B (Deload)**

- **Press-Up** — 2 sets of 8 reps
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 2 sets of 12 reps
- **Reverse Lunge** — 2 sets of 10 reps each leg
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 2 sets of 10 reps each leg
- **Dead Bug** — 2 sets of 8 reps each side
- **Dead Hang** — 2 sets of 30 seconds

Use the extra recovery time this week to focus on sleep, hydration, and mobility work. A twenty-minute yoga or mobility session on the off days is encouraged.

---

## Phase 2 — Weeks 5–8: Strength Development

**Goal:** Build genuine strength through progressive overload, introduce more demanding exercise variations, and begin developing the pulling strength needed for unassisted pull-ups. Volume increases meaningfully, and sessions become more challenging.

**Training Structure:** The programme shifts to an **upper/lower split** across three sessions per week, rotating as follows: Upper A, Lower A, Upper B in week one of the cycle, then Lower B, Upper A, Lower A in week two, and so on. This allows each pattern to be trained roughly twice per week while managing fatigue.

**Tempo Note:** Tempo in Phase 2 is **2-1-1** for most exercises, with specific exceptions noted. The client should now be focused on quality contraction rather than just controlling the movement.

---

### Week 5

**Upper A**

Warm-up: Five minutes of arm circles, band pull-aparts (if a resistance band is available) or scapular pull-ups, and thoracic rotations.

- **Press-Up** — 4 sets of 10 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Chin-Up Negative** (underhand grip, 5-second lower) — 4 sets of 4 reps, 2 minutes rest
- **Inverted Row** (body more horizontal than Phase 1 — feet elevated on a chair if possible) — 3 sets of 10 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Pike Press-Up** (hips high, pressing crown of head toward floor — shoulder emphasis) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Hollow Body Hold** — 3 sets of 20 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 2 sets of 15 reps (warm-down/accessory)

**Lower A**

Warm-up: Hip circles, leg swings, slow bodyweight squats.

- **Bulgarian Split Squat** (rear foot elevated on chair or sofa) — 4 sets of 8 reps each leg, 2-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest between legs
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 4 sets of 15 reps each leg, 2-1-1 tempo, 60 seconds rest
- **Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets of 12 reps each leg, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Wall Sit** — 3 sets of 30 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets of 10 reps each side, 60 seconds rest
- **Calf Raise** (single leg, using wall for balance) — 3 sets of 15 reps each leg, 60 seconds rest

**Upper B**

- **Wide Press-Up** (hands wider than shoulder width, chest emphasis) — 4 sets of 10 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Chin-Up Negative** — 4 sets of 4 reps, 5-second lower, 2 minutes rest
- **Inverted Row** — 3 sets of 12 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Diamond Press-Up** (hands close together, tricep emphasis) — 3 sets of 8 reps, 2-1-1 tempo, 75 seconds rest
- **Side Plank with Hip Dip** — 3 sets of 10 reps each side, 60 seconds rest
- **Dead Hang** — 3 sets of 35 seconds, 90 seconds rest

---

### Week 6

Volume increases. The client adds one set to the primary exercises in each session and increases reps where noted.

**Upper A**

- **Press-Up** — 4 sets of 12 reps, 2-1-1 tempo
- **Chin-Up Negative** — 4 sets of 5 reps, 5-second lower
- **Inverted Row** (feet elevated) — 4 sets of 10 reps
- **Pike Press-Up** — 3 sets of 10 reps
- **Hollow Body Hold** — 3 sets of 25 seconds
- **Scapular Pull-Up** — 2 sets of 15 reps

**Lower A**

- **Bulgarian Split Squat** — 4 sets of 10 reps each leg
- **Single-Leg Glute Bridge** — 4 sets of 15 reps each leg
- **Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets of 15 reps each leg
- **Wall Sit** — 3 sets of 40 seconds
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets of 12 reps each side
- **Single-Leg Calf Raise** — 3 sets of 20 reps each leg

# Nutrition Plan Addition
### Integrated with 12-Week Home Strength Programme

---

## Nutrition Philosophy

The goal here is not to turn your client into a calorie-counting machine. Beginners who are simultaneously learning to train and learning to eat tend to do better with **clear, simple principles** that build gradually into more precise habits. This plan is therefore structured in tiers — foundational habits first, then refinement as the weeks progress, mirroring exactly what we are doing in the gym. By week twelve he should be eating with genuine nutritional intelligence rather than just following rules he does not understand.

The three nutritional priorities for this client, in order of importance, are:

1. **Eating enough protein** to support muscle protein synthesis and recovery
2. **Eating enough total calories** to support training without excessive fat gain
3. **Eating food quality that supports energy, sleep, and long-term adherence**

Everything else — meal timing, micronutrient optimisation, supplementation — sits below these three priorities and will be addressed once the foundations are solid.

---

## Establishing Baseline Numbers

Before prescribing anything, you need to establish where the client currently sits. Ask him to log everything he eats for **three days** before the programme starts — two weekdays and one weekend day — using a free app such as MyFitnessPal or Cronometer. He does not need to change anything yet, just observe. This gives you a genuine baseline rather than a theoretical starting point.

### Estimated Targets

For a 27-year-old beginner male of average build beginning a three-day-per-week strength programme, the following targets provide a reasonable starting framework. These should be adjusted based on his actual body weight, height, and the three-day food log once you receive it.

**Calorie Target:** Bodyweight in kilograms multiplied by 33–35. This places him in a modest caloric surplus sufficient to support muscle growth without excessive fat accumulation. For a 75kg male, this equates to approximately 2,475–2,625 calories per day. If he is currently eating significantly below this, do not jump straight to the target — increase by 200 calories per week to avoid digestive discomfort and psychological overwhelm.

**Protein Target:** 1.8–2.2 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day. For a 75kg male, this is 135–165 grams of protein daily. This range is well-supported by the current sports nutrition literature for natural trainees in a caloric surplus pursuing muscle hypertrophy. Hitting the lower end of this range consistently is far more valuable than occasionally hitting the upper end.

**Carbohydrate Target:** Approximately 45–55% of total calories. Carbohydrates are the primary fuel for the type of training in this programme and should not be feared or restricted. For a 2,500-calorie diet, this means roughly 280–340 grams of carbohydrates per day.

**Fat Target:** The remainder of calories after protein and carbohydrates are accounted for. This typically falls between 25–35% of total calories, or roughly 70–95 grams per day at the 2,500-calorie level. Fat intake should not drop below 0.8 grams per kilogram of bodyweight, as this begins to impair hormonal function including testosterone production, which is directly relevant to muscle building.

---

## Phase 1 Nutrition — Weeks 1–4: Building the Foundation

The nutritional focus in Phase 1 mirrors the training focus: establish habits, build awareness, and do not overcomplicate things. The client has two primary tasks this month.

### Task 1: Hit Protein Every Day

This is the single most important nutritional habit he can build. Everything else is secondary. Protein is the raw material for muscle repair and growth, and most beginners are significantly under-eating it. The target is a minimum of **1.8 grams per kilogram of bodyweight** every single day, including rest days. Muscle is built during recovery, not during training, and protein availability on rest days matters just as much as on training days.

To make this practical, give him a list of high-protein foods with approximate protein content per standard serving. He should aim to include a protein source at every meal and at least one high-protein snack.

**High-Protein Food Reference Guide**

- Chicken breast, 150g cooked — approximately 45g protein
- Tinned tuna, one standard tin (145g drained) — approximately 34g protein
- Eggs, two large — approximately 12g protein
- Greek yoghurt, 200g full-fat — approximately 18g protein
- Cottage cheese, 200g — approximately 22g protein
- Tinned salmon, 145g drained — approximately 30g protein
- Lean beef mince, 150g cooked — approximately 38g protein
- Tofu, firm, 200g — approximately 20g protein
- Lentils, 200g cooked — approximately 18g protein
- Milk, 300ml full-fat — approximately 10g protein
- Protein powder, one scoop (30g) — approximately 22–25g protein depending on brand

### Task 2: Eat Three Solid Meals Per Day

Before worrying about meal timing, supplements, or food quality optimisation, the client simply needs to be eating three structured meals every day. Skipping meals — particularly breakfast — is one of the most common reasons beginners fail to hit their calorie and protein targets. Each meal should contain a protein source, a carbohydrate source, and a vegetable or fruit. That is the entire rule for Phase 1 meals.

### Sample Day of Eating — Phase 1

**Breakfast**

Three scrambled eggs cooked in a teaspoon of olive oil, two slices of wholegrain toast, a large handful of spinach wilted in the pan, and a glass of full-fat milk or a 200g pot of Greek yoghurt on the side. This meal provides approximately 45–50 grams of protein and 550–600 calories.

**Lunch**

A large bowl of pasta (approximately 80g dry weight) with tinned tuna, cherry tomatoes, cucumber, a tablespoon of olive oil, and lemon juice. Alternatively, two wholegrain wraps filled with chicken breast, avocado, mixed leaves, and a light dressing. Either option provides approximately 40–45 grams of protein and 600–650 calories.

**Dinner**

150g of lean beef mince or chicken thighs cooked with onion, garlic, tinned tomatoes, and mixed vegetables, served over 200g of cooked rice or with two medium sweet potatoes. This provides approximately 45–50 grams of protein and 650–700 calories.

**Snack**

200g of cottage cheese with a piece of fruit, or a protein shake made with one scoop of protein powder and 300ml of milk. This adds approximately 25–35 grams of protein and 200–300 calories.

**Daily Total (approximate):** 155–180g protein, 2,000–2,250 calories. This sits at the lower end of the target range, which is appropriate for the first two weeks as the client adjusts. From week three onwards, encourage him to increase portion sizes slightly or add a second snack to push toward the upper end of the calorie target.

### Hydration in Phase 1

Hydration is often overlooked in beginner programmes but has a direct impact on training performance, recovery, and even appetite regulation. The client should aim for a minimum of **2.5–3 litres of water per day**, increasing to **3–3.5 litres on training days**. A practical rule: drink 500ml of water upon waking before consuming anything else, carry a water bottle throughout the day, and drink 400–500ml in the hour before training.

Limit alcohol to a maximum of two standard drinks per week during the programme. Alcohol impairs muscle protein synthesis, disrupts sleep architecture, and adds empty calories that displace more nutritious food. This is not about being puritanical — it is about giving the programme the best possible chance of working.

### Week 4 Deload Nutrition

During the deload week, training volume drops but **nutrition should not drop with it**. This is a common mistake. The body is actively repairing and adapting during the deload, and protein and calorie intake should remain at the same level as training weeks. If anything, the extra recovery time makes this week an ideal opportunity to focus on food quality and meal preparation habits.

---

## Phase 2 Nutrition — Weeks 5–8: Refinement and Precision

With the foundational habits established, Phase 2 introduces more precise nutritional strategies that align with the increased training demands of the upper/lower split.

### Introducing Meal Timing

Meal timing is not as critical as total daily intake, but it becomes meaningfully relevant once the basics are in place. The following timing guidelines will support training performance and recovery without requiring the client to restructure his entire day.

**Pre-Training Meal:** The client should eat a balanced meal containing both protein and carbohydrates **two to three hours before training**. This ensures glycogen stores are topped up and amino acids are available in the bloodstream during the session. If he trains early in the morning and a full meal is not practical, a smaller snack of 30–40 grams of carbohydrates and 20 grams of protein consumed 45–60 minutes before training is an acceptable alternative. A banana with a glass of milk, or a small bowl of oats with a scoop of protein powder, both work well.

**Post-Training Meal:** The post-workout window is real but not as narrow as fitness culture often suggests. The client should aim to eat a protein-rich meal within **two hours of finishing training**. This meal should contain 40–50 grams of protein and a substantial carbohydrate source to begin replenishing glycogen. The sample dinner above is an ideal post-training meal. If training late in the evening and a full meal is not practical, a protein shake with milk and a banana is a sufficient bridge until the next day.

**Pre-Sleep Protein:** This is one of the most underutilised strategies in beginner nutrition. Consuming 30–40 grams of slow-digesting protein — specifically casein protein, found naturally in cottage cheese, Greek yoghurt, and milk — in the 30–60 minutes before sleep has been shown in multiple studies to increase overnight muscle protein synthesis. The client should add a pre-sleep snack of 200g of cottage cheese or Greek yoghurt, or a casein protein shake if he uses supplements. This is particularly important on training days.

### Increasing Calorie Target

By week five, the client should be comfortable hitting his Phase 1 calorie range consistently. Now is the time to push toward the upper end of the target — **bodyweight multiplied by 35** — to ensure he is providing sufficient energy for the increased training volume. If he has been gaining weight at a rate faster than 0.5–1kg per month, pull back slightly toward the lower end of the range. If he has gained nothing in four weeks of training and eating, push toward the upper end or slightly above it.

### Carbohydrate Cycling — A Simple Introduction

Full carbohydrate cycling is unnecessarily complex for a beginner, but a simplified version is worth introducing in Phase 2. The principle is straightforward: eat more carbohydrates on training days when the body needs fuel and can use them efficiently, and slightly fewer on rest days when energy demands are lower.

**Training Day Carbohydrate Target:** Upper end of the 280–340 gram range.

**Rest Day Carbohydrate Target:** Lower end of the range, approximately 220–260 grams. Protein and fat intake remain the same on rest days.

This does not require precise tracking if the client is resistant to it. A simpler version is: on training days, have an extra portion of rice, pasta, oats, or bread. On rest days, replace one of those carbohydrate portions with extra vegetables. The principle is the same even if the execution is approximate.

### Food Quality Upgrade

Phase 2 is also the time to audit food quality. The client should aim for the following targets by the end of week eight.

**Vegetables and Fruit:** A minimum of five portions per day, aiming for variety in colour. Dark leafy greens such as spinach, kale, and broccoli should feature at least once daily for their micronutrient density. Vegetables are not just health food — the vitamins and minerals they provide, particularly magnesium, zinc, and vitamin C, directly support testosterone production, immune function, and recovery.

**Whole Grains Over Refined Grains:** Swap white bread for wholegrain, white rice for brown rice or basmati, and regular pasta for wholegrain pasta where possible. This is not a strict rule — white rice and white pasta are not harmful — but whole grain versions provide more fibre, more micronutrients, and better satiety per calorie.

**Healthy Fats:** Ensure fat intake includes sources of omega-3 fatty acids, which have anti-inflammatory properties relevant to training recovery. Oily fish such as salmon, mackerel, and sardines should appear two to three times per week. If the client dislikes fish, a daily fish oil supplement providing 1–2 grams of combined EPA and DHA is a reasonable alternative.

**Limit Ultra-Processed Foods:** This does not mean eliminating them. It means being honest about frequency. If the client is eating ultra-processed foods — crisps, fast food, sugary cereals, processed meats — more than three or four times per week, it is worth having a conversation about substitutions rather than restrictions. The goal is crowding out poor choices with better ones, not creating a forbidden foods list that breeds obsession.

### Sample Day of Eating — Phase 2 (Training Day)

**Breakfast (approximately 2–3 hours before training)**

80g of rolled oats cooked with 300ml of full-fat milk, topped with a tablespoon of peanut butter, a sliced banana, and a teaspoon of honey. Two boiled eggs on the side. Approximately 55g protein, 95g carbohydrates, 700 calories.

**Lunch**

200g of cooked chicken breast sliced over a large mixed salad with quinoa (80g cooked), cherry tomatoes, cucumber, roasted red peppers, and a dressing of olive oil and balsamic vinegar. Approximately 50g protein, 60g carbohydrates, 600 calories.

**Post-Training Dinner**

150g of salmon fillet baked in the oven with lemon and herbs, served with 250g of cooked sweet potato and a large portion of steamed broccoli and green beans. Approximately 45g protein, 65g carbohydrates, 600 calories.

**Pre-Sleep Snack**

200g of full-fat cottage cheese with a small handful of mixed berries and a drizzle of honey. Approximately 25g protein, 20g carbohydrates, 220 calories.

**Daily Total (approximate):** 175g protein, 240g carbohydrates, 75g fat, 2,120 calories. Add a mid-afternoon snack of a protein shake or Greek yoghurt to push toward the 2,500-calorie target.

### Week 8 Deload Nutrition

Same principle as Week 4 — maintain protein and calories. Use the reduced training load to meal prep for Phase 3, which is the most demanding phase of the programme.

---

## Phase 3 Nutrition — Weeks 9–12: Performance Nutrition

Phase 3 is where the client should feel the clearest connection between what he eats and how he performs. Sessions are longer, more intense, and more technically demanding. Nutrition in this phase is explicitly performance-focused.

### Calorie Adjustment for Phase 3

Reassess calorie intake at the start of week nine. If the client has been gaining weight at a healthy rate of 0.5–1kg per month and feels energetic in training, maintain current intake. If he has been gaining faster than this, reduce by 150–200 calories per day, primarily from carbohydrates. If he has been gaining slower than this or feels flat and fatigued in sessions, increase by 150–200 calories per day, again primarily from carbohydrates.

### Pre-Training Nutrition Becomes Critical

In Phase 3, the client is attempting maximum-effort pull-ups, heavy Bulgarian split squats, and Nordic curls. Arriving at these sessions under-fuelled will directly compromise performance and increase injury risk. The pre-training meal protocol from Phase 2 should now be treated as non-negotiable. If he has been skipping pre-training meals, this is the conversation to have at the start of week nine.

### Creatine Monohydrate

Phase 3 is the appropriate time to introduce the one supplement that has the most robust evidence base in sports nutrition. Creatine monohydrate has been studied for over thirty years and consistently demonstrates improvements in strength, power output, and lean mass in resistance-trained individuals. It is safe, inexpensive, and effective.

**Protocol:** 3–5 grams of creatine monohydrate per day, taken at any time, with food or a protein shake. There is no need for a loading phase. Consistent daily intake is all that is required. Effects become noticeable after approximately two to four weeks of consistent use. The client should expect a small initial increase in body weight of 0.5–1.5kg due to increased intramuscular water retention — this is normal and desirable, as it reflects increased creatine storage in the muscles.

### Managing Fatigue Nutritionally

Phase 3 will produce more accumulated fatigue than any previous phase. Two nutritional strategies help manage this.

**Increase Carbohydrate Intake Around Sessions:** On training days in Phase 3, the client should add an additional 30–50 grams of fast-digesting carbohydrates immediately post-training. A banana, a glass of fruit juice, or a handful of dried fruit alongside his post-training protein source will accelerate glycogen replenishment and reduce next-day soreness.

**Prioritise Iron and Magnesium:** Fatigue that persists beyond 48 hours after training, poor sleep quality, and low mood can all be signs of micronutrient insufficiency. Magnesium in particular is depleted through sweat and is commonly under-consumed. Encourage the client to eat magnesium-rich foods daily: dark chocolate, pumpkin seeds, spinach, almonds, and black beans are all excellent sources. If sleep quality is poor, a magnesium glycinate supplement of 200–400mg taken before bed is worth considering.

A four-egg omelette with spinach, mushrooms, and feta cheese, cooked in olive oil. Two slices of sourdough toast with avocado. A glass of orange juice. Approximately 50g protein, 70g carbohydrates, 700 calories.

**Mid-Morning Snack**

A protein shake made with one scoop of whey protein, 300ml of full-fat milk, a tablespoon of peanut butter, and a banana blended together. Approximately 40g protein, 55g carbohydrates, 450 calories.

**Lunch (Pre-Training Meal, 2–3 hours before session)**

200g of lean beef mince cooked with onion, garlic, and mixed herbs, served over 250g of cooked basmati rice with a side of roasted vegetables. Approximately 50g protein, 80g carbohydrates, 650 calories.

**Immediate Post-Training**

A banana and 500ml of milk, or a protein shake with a banana. Approximately 25–30g protein, 40g carbohydrates, 300 calories.

**Dinner**

150g of chicken thighs roasted with olive oil and herbs, served with 300g of roasted sweet potato and a large mixed salad with olive oil dressing. Approximately 45g protein, 70g carbohydrates, 600 calories.

**Pre-Sleep Snack**

200g of Greek yoghurt with a tablespoon of honey and a small handful of walnuts. Approximately 20g protein, 25g carbohydrates, 280 calories.

---

## Supplement Summary

Supplements are the last priority, not the first. The following list represents everything worth considering for this client, ranked by evidence quality and practical relevance.

**Tier 1 — Worth Taking**

- **Creatine Monohydrate:** 3–5g daily from week nine onwards, as described above.
- **Vitamin D3:** 1,000–2,000 IU daily, particularly if the client lives in a northern climate or spends limited time outdoors. Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common and impairs testosterone production, immune function, and mood.
- **Protein Powder (Whey or Plant-Based):** Not a supplement in the traditional sense, but a convenient food source. Useful if the client struggles to hit protein targets through whole food alone. One to two scoops per day maximum — whole food protein sources should always be the priority.

**Tier 2 — Consider Based on Individual Need**

- **Magnesium Glycinate:** 200–400mg before bed if sleep quality is poor or fatigue is persistent.
- **Fish Oil:** 1–2g of combined EPA and DHA daily if oily fish intake is below two portions per week.
- **Zinc:** 15–25mg daily if the client eats little red meat or shellfish. Zinc is critical for testosterone production and immune function.

**Tier 3 — Not Necessary**

Pre-workout stimulants, BCAAs, glutamine, testosterone boosters, and fat burners are all unnecessary for this client at this stage. Pre-workout caffeine is the one exception — a cup of coffee 30–45 minutes before training is a legitimate, evidence-backed performance enhancer. It is also free and already in most people's kitchens.

---

## Tracking and Check-In Protocol

To make this nutrition plan actionable for a remote coaching relationship, establish the following check-in structure.

**Weekly:** The client sends you a brief message noting his average daily protein intake for the week (tracked via app or estimated), his body weight measured on the same morning under the same conditions, and a subjective energy rating out of ten for training sessions that week.

**Every Four Weeks:** A more detailed review at the end of each phase. Compare body weight trend, training performance, and how the client feels. Adjust calorie targets based on the rate of weight change. If he has gained more than 1.5kg in a month, reduce calories slightly. If he has gained less than 0.3kg and performance is stagnant, increase calories.

**The One Rule Above All Others:** If the client can only do one thing from this entire nutrition plan, it should be hitting his protein target every single day. Calories, timing, food quality, and supplements all matter, but none of them matter as much as consistent, adequate protein intake. Build that habit first, and everything else becomes easier to layer on top.

# Cardio Addition
### Integrated with 12-Week Home Strength Programme and Nutrition Plan

---

## Cardio Philosophy

Before prescribing a single cardio session, it is worth being explicit about the role cardio plays in this specific programme. Your client is a beginner pursuing strength development in a small flat with minimal equipment. That context shapes everything about how cardio should be programmed here.

The primary risk with adding cardio to a beginner strength programme is **interference**. When cardiovascular training volume is too high, too intense, or too poorly timed relative to strength sessions, it competes with strength adaptation for recovery resources. The body has a finite capacity to adapt, and asking it to simultaneously become significantly stronger and significantly more aerobically fit is a harder ask than fitness culture typically acknowledges. This does not mean cardio should be avoided — it means it should be programmed intelligently, with the strength work always treated as the priority.

The secondary consideration is space. A small flat rules out running in place for extended periods without disturbing neighbours, rules out large jumping movements on hard floors without appropriate matting, and generally demands low-impact or controlled-impact solutions. Every cardio session in this plan is designed with that constraint in mind.

The cardio in this programme serves four distinct purposes across the twelve weeks, and understanding these purposes will help you explain the reasoning to your client rather than just handing him a list of exercises.

**Weeks 1–4:** Cardio builds aerobic base and improves work capacity, making strength sessions feel less breathless and recovery between sets faster.

**Weeks 5–8:** Cardio develops cardiovascular efficiency and begins contributing meaningfully to body composition alongside the strength work.

**Weeks 9–12:** Cardio is used strategically to enhance performance in strength sessions and to build the kind of general fitness that extends beyond the programme itself.

---

## Cardio Structure Overview

Cardio sessions are programmed on **non-strength training days** wherever possible. With three strength sessions per week, this leaves three to four days available for cardio. The client will not perform cardio every available day — recovery is a training variable, not dead time. The weekly cardio prescription is as follows.

**Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4):** Two cardio sessions per week, both low-to-moderate intensity.

**Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8):** Two to three cardio sessions per week, introducing one moderate-to-high intensity session alongside the lower intensity work.

**Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12):** Two to three cardio sessions per week, with one high-intensity session, one moderate session, and one optional active recovery session.

The three cardio modalities used throughout this programme are defined below. Understanding these modalities is more important than memorising specific sessions, because they give the client a framework he can apply independently after week twelve.

---

## The Three Cardio Modalities

### Modality 1: Low-Intensity Steady State (LISS)

Low-intensity steady state cardio is performed at a conversational pace — the client should be able to speak in full sentences throughout. Heart rate sits at approximately 50–65% of maximum, which for a 27-year-old equates to roughly 97–126 beats per minute. In a flat, this means sustained low-impact movement for a continuous duration.

LISS is the backbone of the cardio programme in Phase 1 and remains present throughout all twelve weeks. It builds aerobic base without generating significant fatigue, supports active recovery by increasing blood flow to sore muscles, and is sustainable enough to perform the day after a hard strength session without compromising the next session.

**Home LISS Options:**

- **Walking in place with high knees** — a surprisingly effective option that generates minimal noise and impact. The client lifts his knees to hip height with each step, swings his arms naturally, and maintains a steady rhythm. This is not marching — the movement should feel fluid and continuous.
- **Step-touch side to side** — stepping laterally from foot to foot with a light arm swing. Completely silent, zero impact, and sustainable for long durations.
- **Stair climbing** — if the flat has internal stairs or access to a stairwell, walking up and down continuously is one of the most effective low-impact cardio options available. Even a single flight of stairs used repeatedly for twenty minutes provides meaningful cardiovascular stimulus.
- **Shadow boxing at low intensity** — moving around the mat space, throwing light punches, shifting weight from foot to foot. Keeps the heart rate elevated without impact and has the added benefit of being genuinely enjoyable for many people.
- **Yoga flow or mobility-based movement** — a structured yoga sequence performed continuously at a pace that keeps the heart rate mildly elevated counts as LISS and doubles as flexibility and recovery work.

### Modality 2: Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training (MICT)

Moderate-intensity continuous training sits at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, approximately 126–146 beats per minute for a 27-year-old. At this intensity, conversation becomes effortful — the client can speak in short sentences but not comfortably. Sessions are shorter than LISS, typically 20–35 minutes, and generate more meaningful cardiovascular adaptation.

MICT is introduced in Phase 2 and requires slightly more recovery than LISS. It should not be performed the day before a demanding strength session if it can be avoided.

**Home MICT Options:**

- **Continuous bodyweight circuit** — moving through a sequence of low-impact exercises without stopping, maintaining a steady elevated heart rate throughout. The circuit is not performed for maximum reps but at a controlled, continuous pace. Example circuit: step-touch for 60 seconds, bodyweight squat for 60 seconds, mountain climbers for 30 seconds, press-up for 30 seconds, repeat.
- **Dance or aerobics-style movement** — following a YouTube aerobics or dance workout at moderate intensity. This is a legitimate training tool and the client should not be embarrassed about it. Many of the most effective home cardio workouts available online are aerobics-based.
- **Skipping** — if the client has a skipping rope and sufficient ceiling height, skipping at a moderate pace is one of the most time-efficient cardio options available. Even without a rope, simulated skipping — performing the arm and foot movement without the rope — elevates heart rate effectively.
- **Continuous stair climbing at a brisker pace** — the same stair option as LISS but performed faster, taking stairs two at a time or increasing the pace to push heart rate into the moderate zone.

### Modality 3: High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)

HIIT involves alternating between periods of near-maximal effort and periods of active recovery or complete rest. Work intervals push heart rate to 85–95% of maximum — the client should be unable to speak more than a word or two. Rest intervals allow partial recovery before the next work bout.

HIIT is the most time-efficient cardio modality and produces the greatest acute metabolic disturbance, meaning it continues to burn calories at an elevated rate for hours after the session ends. However, it also generates the most fatigue and should be treated with the same respect as a hard strength session. In this programme, HIIT appears only once per week from Phase 2 onwards, and never on the day before or after a strength session.

**Home HIIT Options:**

All HIIT options below are designed to be performable on a yoga mat in a small flat with minimal noise and impact. True jumping movements are included as options but flagged for noise sensitivity.

- **Burpee variations** — the standard burpee is highly effective but noisy on hard floors. A modified burpee — stepping feet back to plank rather than jumping, and stepping back in rather than jumping up — retains most of the cardiovascular benefit with a fraction of the impact.
- **Mountain climbers** — performed on the mat, driving knees toward the chest alternately at high speed. Completely silent, highly effective, and scalable by adjusting pace.
- **Squat thrusts** — similar to mountain climbers but both feet move simultaneously. High heart rate stimulus with manageable noise.
- **High knees at speed** — running in place with knees driving to hip height as fast as possible. Moderate impact — the client should wear trainers and use the yoga mat.
- **Press-up to plank jack** — perform a press-up, then from the top position jump or step feet wide and back in rapidly. Combines upper body and cardiovascular stimulus.
- **Lateral shuffle** — moving rapidly side to side across the mat space, touching the floor at each end. Low impact, high heart rate.
- **Tuck jumps** — only if the client has adequate ceiling height and the floor situation permits. The most intense option available.

---

## Phase 1 Cardio — Weeks 1–4: Building the Engine

**Prescription:** Two LISS sessions per week, each 20–30 minutes, on non-strength training days.

The goal in Phase 1 is simply to establish the habit of cardio and begin building aerobic base. Sessions are deliberately easy. If the client finds them too easy, that is correct — Phase 1 cardio is not supposed to be challenging. It is supposed to be consistent.

### Week 1 Cardio

**Session 1 — LISS Walk (20 minutes)**

The client performs continuous walking in place with high knees for the full twenty minutes. To make this more structured and less monotonous, divide the session into four five-minute blocks with a brief posture check between each block. During each block, the client focuses on a different aspect of movement: block one is relaxed arms, block two is deliberate breathing through the nose, block three is slightly higher knee drive, block four is maintaining pace while consciously relaxing the shoulders. Play music or a podcast to make the time pass.

**Session 2 — LISS Shadow Boxing (20 minutes)**

The client moves continuously around the mat space for twenty minutes, throwing light punches and shifting his weight from foot to foot. No technique is required — this is purely about sustained movement. Divide into four five-minute rounds with thirty seconds of rest between rounds. During rest periods, shake out the arms and take three deep breaths.

### Week 2 Cardio

Both sessions extend to 25 minutes. The structure remains the same but duration increases.

**Session 1 — LISS Walk (25 minutes)**

As week one but five minutes longer. The client should notice that 25 minutes feels manageable — this is the aerobic base beginning to develop.

**Session 2 — LISS Mobility Flow (25 minutes)**

Replace the shadow boxing session this week with a continuous mobility flow. The client moves through the following sequence without stopping, holding each position for the prescribed time before flowing to the next. The sequence repeats for the full 25 minutes.

- Cat-cow on the mat — 8 slow repetitions
- Child's pose — 20 seconds
- Downward dog — 20 seconds
- Hip flexor stretch, right leg forward — 20 seconds
- Hip flexor stretch, left leg forward — 20 seconds
- Seated hamstring stretch — 20 seconds
- Thoracic rotation, right — 10 seconds
- Thoracic rotation, left — 10 seconds
- Return to cat-cow

This session doubles as recovery work for the strength training and is particularly valuable after the leg sessions.

### Week 3 Cardio

Sessions extend to 30 minutes. A very light introduction to varied intensity is added within the LISS framework — not true MICT, but a gentle preview of what is coming in Phase 2.

**Session 1 — LISS Walk with Effort Surges (30 minutes)**

The client performs his standard walking in place for 30 minutes but every five minutes performs one minute of slightly elevated effort — higher knees, faster arm swing, more deliberate drive. Heart rate should rise slightly during these surges but should not reach a breathless level. This is a 1:4 work-to-easy ratio and is purely introductory.

**Session 2 — LISS Shadow Boxing (30 minutes)**

Return to shadow boxing, now for 30 minutes. The client should find this significantly more manageable than week one's 20-minute session. That improvement is real aerobic adaptation.

### Week 4 Cardio — Deload

During the deload week, cardio reduces to **one session of 20 minutes** at easy LISS pace. No surges, no structure — just 20 minutes of continuous easy movement. Walking in place, shadow boxing, or the mobility flow are all appropriate. The goal is to maintain the habit without adding recovery stress.

---

## Phase 2 Cardio — Weeks 5–8: Building Capacity

**Prescription:** Two to three sessions per week. One LISS session of 30–35 minutes, one MICT session of 20–25 minutes, and one optional HIIT session of 15–20 minutes introduced from week six onwards.

The cardio programme now has genuine structure and variety. The client is training three days per week for strength, which means a typical week looks like this.

**Example Week Structure — Phase 2**

- Monday: Strength — Upper A
- Tuesday: LISS (30 minutes)
- Wednesday: Strength — Lower A
- Thursday: MICT (20–25 minutes)
- Friday: Strength — Upper B
- Saturday: HIIT (15–20 minutes, from week six) or rest
- Sunday: Complete rest

This structure ensures no cardio session falls immediately before a strength session, and the HIIT session is separated from strength work by at least one day on each side.

### Week 5 Cardio

**LISS Session — 30 minutes**

The client performs 30 minutes of continuous low-intensity movement. Introduce a new option this week: **continuous step-touch with arm variations**. The client steps side to side continuously while cycling through different arm movements every two minutes — arms forward, arms overhead, arms in a rowing motion, arms in a punching motion. This adds upper body engagement and prevents the monotony that can derail LISS compliance.

**MICT Session — 20 minutes**

Introduce the first true MICT session using the following continuous bodyweight circuit. The client moves through each exercise for the prescribed time without stopping, then repeats the circuit for the full 20 minutes. The pace should be controlled and continuous — this is not a race.

- Step-touch side to side — 60 seconds
- Bodyweight squat at moderate pace — 60 seconds
- Mountain climbers — 30 seconds
- Press-up at moderate pace — 30 seconds
- Walking in place with high knees — 60 seconds
- Glute bridge, continuous reps — 60 seconds
- Step-touch side to side — 60 seconds

One full circuit takes approximately seven minutes. The client completes two to three full circuits in the 20-minute window. Rest is not prescribed between exercises — if he needs to slow down, he slows down rather than stopping.

### Week 6 Cardio

**LISS Session — 35 minutes**

Duration increases to 35 minutes. The client can choose any LISS modality he has enjoyed so far. Encourage him to use this session as active recovery — it should feel restorative, not taxing.

**MICT Session — 25 minutes**

The circuit from week five extends to 25 minutes. Add one additional exercise to the circuit: **lateral shuffle** for 45 seconds between the mountain climbers and press-up blocks.

**HIIT Session — 15 minutes (introduced this week)**

This is the first true HIIT session of the programme. Keep it short and introduce the format carefully. The session uses a simple **20 seconds on, 40 seconds off** protocol — a 1:2 work-to-rest ratio that is appropriate for a beginner to HIIT.

Warm up for three minutes with easy walking in place and arm circles before beginning.

- **Round 1:** Modified burpees — 20 seconds work, 40 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.
- **Round 2:** Mountain climbers — 20 seconds work, 40 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.
- **Round 3:** High knees — 20 seconds work, 40 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.

Cool down for three minutes with slow walking and deep breathing. Total session time including warm-up and cool-down is approximately 18–20 minutes.

The client should feel genuinely breathless during work intervals. If he does not, the pace is too slow. If he cannot complete the work intervals, the pace is too fast — scale back and build up.

### Week 7 Cardio

**LISS Session — 35 minutes**

Maintain duration. Introduce **shadow boxing with footwork patterns** as an option — the client moves around the mat space using specific footwork: forward-back, side-side, and circular movement, throwing punches continuously. This is more engaging than walking in place and develops coordination alongside cardiovascular fitness.

**MICT Session — 25 minutes**

Increase the pace of the circuit slightly. The client should be working at a level where conversation is effortful. Add **squat thrusts** for 30 seconds between the glute bridge and final step-touch blocks.

**HIIT Session — 18 minutes**

Progress the HIIT protocol to **30 seconds on, 30 seconds off** — a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio. This is meaningfully harder than the previous week.

Warm up for three minutes.

- **Round 1:** Modified burpees — 30 seconds work, 30 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.
- **Round 2:** Mountain climbers — 30 seconds work, 30 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.
- **Round 3:** High knees — 30 seconds work, 30 seconds rest. Repeat 4 times.
- **Round 4:** Press-up to plank jack — 30 seconds work, 30 seconds rest. Repeat 3 times.

Cool down for three minutes. Total time approximately 20–22 minutes.

### Week 8 Cardio — Deload

Reduce to **one LISS session of 25 minutes** and **one MICT session of 15 minutes** at reduced intensity. No HIIT this week. The deload applies to cardio just as it applies to strength training.

---

## Phase 3 Cardio — Weeks 9–12: Performance Cardio

**Prescription:** Two to three sessions per week. One HIIT session, one MICT session, and one optional LISS active recovery session. Total cardio volume is managed carefully to avoid interfering with the most demanding strength phase of the programme.

**Critical Note for Phase 3:** The strength sessions in weeks nine through twelve are the hardest of the entire programme. Pull-up attempts, Nordic curls, and decline press-ups all demand significant recovery. If the client reports persistent fatigue, poor sleep, or declining strength performance, the first adjustment is to reduce cardio volume — drop the MICT session first, then reduce HIIT duration. Strength performance is the priority.

### Week 9 Cardio

**HIIT Session — 20 minutes**

Progress to a **40 seconds on, 20 seconds off** protocol — a 2:1 work-to-rest ratio. This is the most demanding HIIT format in the programme and should be treated accordingly.

Warm up for four minutes: two minutes of easy walking in place, one minute of arm circles and hip rotations, one minute of slow bodyweight squats.

Perform four rounds of the following circuit. Each exercise is performed for 40 seconds with 20 seconds rest before moving to the next.

- Modified burpee
- Mountain climbers
- High knees
- Lateral shuffle
- Squat thrust
- Press-up to plank jack

Rest for 90 seconds between full circuit rounds. Complete three to four full rounds depending on fitness level. Cool down for three minutes.

**MICT Session — 25 minutes**

The client now has enough fitness to perform a more structured MICT session. Introduce **Tabata-style moderate work** — not true Tabata, which is maximal effort, but a moderate-intensity version using the same time structure.

Perform the following sequence continuously for 25 minutes, cycling through the exercises at a pace that keeps heart rate in the 65–75% zone.

- Step-touch — 2 minutes
- Bodyweight squat — 90 seconds
- Mountain climbers — 60 seconds
- Shadow boxing — 2 minutes
- Lateral shuffle — 90 seconds
- Walking lunge — 60 seconds
- Repeat from the top

**Optional LISS Session — 30 minutes**

On a day when the client feels fatigued but wants to move, a 30-minute LISS session of his choice. This is explicitly optional and should be skipped if he is tired.

### Week 10 Cardio

**HIIT Session — 22 minutes**

Maintain the 40:20 protocol but add one additional exercise to the circuit: **tuck jumps** or, if noise is a concern, **squat jumps performed with a soft landing** — the client bends his knees deeply on landing to absorb impact quietly. This is the most explosive movement in the entire programme and should only be included if the client's joints feel healthy and the floor situation permits.

If jumping is not appropriate, substitute **speed mountain climbers** — mountain climbers performed as fast as possible for the full 40 seconds.

**MICT Session — 25 minutes**

Maintain the week nine structure. The client should now be completing three full cycles of the circuit within the 25-minute window, which represents meaningful improvement from week five.

### Week 11 Cardio

**HIIT Session — 25 minutes**

The longest and most demanding HIIT session of the programme. Warm up for four minutes.

Perform the following **AMRAP-style HIIT circuit** — as many rounds as possible in 15 minutes of work time, with a 10-second transition between exercises and a 90-second rest after every three rounds.

- Modified burpee — 30 seconds
- Mountain climbers — 30 seconds
- High knees — 30 seconds
- Lateral shuffle — 30 seconds
- Squat thrust — 30 seconds

Track how many complete rounds the client achieves. This becomes a benchmark he can retest in week twelve and beyond.

Cool down for four minutes: slow walking, deep breathing, and full-body stretching.

**MICT Session — 20 minutes**

Reduce MICT duration slightly this week to manage total fatigue load, as week eleven is also the peak strength week. Quality over quantity.

### Week 12 Cardio — Programme Finale

Week twelve is the final week of the programme and should feel like a celebration of everything the client has built. Strength sessions this week include final performance tests — maximum pull-up reps, maximum press-up reps, and so on. Cardio mirrors this with a final benchmark test.

**HIIT Benchmark Retest — 25 minutes**

Repeat the week eleven AMRAP circuit exactly. Same exercises, same timing, same 15-minute work window. The client counts his rounds and compares to week eleven. Improvement here — even one additional round — represents genuine cardiovascular adaptation over twelve weeks.

**Final LISS Session — 30 minutes**

The last cardio session of the programme is a 30-minute LISS session of the client's choice. Encourage him to use this session reflectively — to notice how different 30 minutes of continuous movement feels compared to week one, when 20 minutes was a genuine challenge. That difference is fitness.

---

## Cardio and Nutrition Integration

The cardio additions have implications for the nutrition plan that are worth flagging explicitly.

**Calorie Adjustment for Cardio Days:** On days when the client performs MICT or HIIT, add approximately 150–250 calories to his daily target, primarily from carbohydrates. A banana and a glass of milk before or after the session is a simple way to achieve this without overthinking it. LISS sessions do not require calorie adjustment.

**Hydration on Cardio Days:** Add 500ml of water to the daily hydration target on any day that includes a cardio session. HIIT sessions in particular generate significant sweat loss even in a cool flat.

**Avoid Cardio in a Fasted State:** Particularly in Phase 3, the client should not perform MICT or HIIT sessions without having eaten in the preceding two to three hours. Fasted cardio is a popular concept but has no meaningful advantage for body composition and significantly impairs performance in moderate-to-high intensity sessions. A small carbohydrate-containing snack before cardio is always appropriate.

**Cardio on Deload Weeks:** During weeks four and eight, cardio reduces alongside strength training as described in the phase-specific sections. During these weeks, the LISS mobility flow sessions are particularly valuable as they support recovery without adding stress.

# Equipment Purchasing Guide
### Recommendations for Progressing Beyond Bodyweight Training

---

## The Right Mindset Before Spending Anything

The first thing to tell your client is this: **do not buy anything yet**. Complete the twelve-week programme first. This is not a throwaway comment — it has genuine practical reasoning behind it.

Most beginners dramatically overestimate how quickly they will outgrow bodyweight training and dramatically underestimate how much strength they can build without any equipment at all. By the time he finishes week twelve, he will have a much clearer picture of what his actual training gaps are, what movements he genuinely enjoys, and what his flat can realistically accommodate. Buying equipment before you know these things leads to expensive mistakes — dumbbells that are the wrong weight, a barbell that does not fit the space, a rack that never gets used.

He should also finish the programme knowing that the pull-up bar he already owns is one of the most valuable pieces of training equipment in existence. A person who can perform ten strict pull-ups, twenty press-ups, and single-leg squats with control has built a genuinely impressive strength base. The equipment below is about extending that base, not replacing it.

With that said, when he is ready to invest, here is exactly what to recommend and in what order.

---

## The Priority Purchasing Order

Equipment should be bought in tiers, with each tier only purchased once the previous tier is being used consistently and has become a limiting factor in training. Buying everything at once is wasteful and overwhelming.

---

## Tier 1 — Buy First
### Estimated Cost: £80–£150 Total

These two purchases will transform the programme immediately and represent by far the best return on investment available in home fitness equipment.

### 1. Adjustable Resistance Bands — £20–£40

Resistance bands are the single highest-value purchase available to a home trainer working in a small space. They are lightweight, take up almost no storage space, cost very little, and add an enormous range of exercise options to a bodyweight programme.

For this client specifically, bands serve three immediate purposes. First, they allow **assisted pull-up training** — looping a band around the bar and placing a knee or foot in it reduces the effective bodyweight being lifted, allowing the client to perform more reps with better form and accelerating pull-up strength development beyond what negatives alone can achieve. Second, they add **resistance to bodyweight exercises** — a band looped around the thighs during glute bridges, squats, and lunges adds meaningful load to movements that bodyweight alone will eventually make too easy. Third, they introduce **pulling exercises** that the pull-up bar cannot provide in horizontal planes — seated rows, face pulls, and pull-aparts all become available with a band anchored in a doorframe.

**What to buy:** A set of loop bands in multiple resistances — typically light (approximately 5–15kg resistance), medium (15–35kg), and heavy (35–55kg). Brands worth recommending include Gymshark, Mirafit, and Fit Simplify. Avoid very cheap single-band sets — the resistance range matters. A set of five bands covering light through extra-heavy costs approximately £20–£35 and will last years with basic care.

Additionally, a long resistance band (also called a pull-up assistance band) in a heavy resistance — 50–80kg — is worth buying separately if the set does not include one. This is specifically for pull-up assistance and costs approximately £10–£15 on its own.

### 2. Adjustable Dumbbells — £60–£120

If the client can only buy one piece of weighted equipment, it should be adjustable dumbbells. A single pair of adjustable dumbbells that can be set anywhere from 2kg to 24kg effectively replaces an entire rack of fixed dumbbells and takes up the space of a shoebox.

Adjustable dumbbells immediately unlock a vast range of exercises that bodyweight cannot replicate: dumbbell rows, dumbbell press variations, Romanian deadlifts, goblet squats, lateral raises, bicep curls, tricep extensions, and loaded carries. More importantly, they solve the fundamental limitation of bodyweight training — the inability to add small, precise increments of load to exercises. With dumbbells, progressive overload becomes straightforward and measurable in a way that bodyweight progressions, which require exercise substitutions rather than load additions, cannot match.

**What to buy:** There are two main options depending on budget.

The **budget option** is a pair of fixed-weight dumbbells in two sizes — a lighter pair at 8–10kg and a heavier pair at 14–16kg. This costs approximately £40–£70 depending on retailer and covers most beginner-to-intermediate dumbbell exercises. The limitation is that he will outgrow specific weights and need to buy more over time, which becomes more expensive in the long run.

The **recommended option** is a single pair of **selectorised adjustable dumbbells** such as the Bowflex SelectTech 552, the PowerBlock Sport, or the more affordable Ativafit or Flybird adjustable dumbbell sets. These use a dial or pin mechanism to change weight in seconds and typically adjust from 2–24kg per dumbbell. They cost £80–£150 for a pair but replace what would otherwise be eight to ten pairs of fixed dumbbells. For a small flat, the space saving alone justifies the price difference. The Ativafit 25kg adjustable dumbbell set is a particularly good value option at approximately £90–£110 for the pair.

**A note on second-hand equipment:** Dumbbells hold their value extremely well and are widely available second-hand on Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, and eBay. Fixed-weight dumbbells in particular can often be found for 50–70% below retail price. Encourage the client to check these platforms before buying new — a set of fixed dumbbells at 8kg, 12kg, 16kg, and 20kg bought second-hand will often cost less than a new adjustable set and serve him just as well.

---

## Tier 2 — Buy Second
### Estimated Cost: £50–£120 Total

Once the bands and dumbbells are in regular use and the client is consistently training, these additions extend the programme significantly.

### 3. Kettlebell — £30–£60

A single kettlebell is a remarkably versatile tool that complements dumbbells rather than duplicating them. The offset centre of mass of a kettlebell makes it superior to dumbbells for specific movements — swings, Turkish get-ups, goblet squats, and single-arm carries all feel more natural and effective with a kettlebell than with a dumbbell.

The kettlebell swing in particular is worth highlighting. It is one of the most effective posterior chain exercises available outside of a barbell deadlift, training the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back through a powerful hip hinge pattern that bodyweight exercises struggle to replicate with the same loading. For a client who has been doing glute bridges and Nordic curls, introducing kettlebell swings represents a significant upgrade in hip hinge training quality.

**What to buy:** A single kettlebell at a weight appropriate to his current strength level. After completing the twelve-week programme, most male beginners are well-served by a **16kg kettlebell** as a first purchase. This is heavy enough to make swings genuinely challenging and light enough to learn the movement safely. As he progresses, a second kettlebell at 20–24kg can be added. Brands worth recommending include Mirafit, Wolverson, and Rogue — all produce well-made cast iron kettlebells. Avoid plastic-coated or vinyl kettlebells, which are often poorly balanced. A quality 16kg cast iron kettlebell costs approximately £30–£50 new and is widely available second-hand.

### 4. Gymnastic Rings — £25–£45

Gymnastic rings are one of the most underrated pieces of home training equipment available. They hang from the existing pull-up bar using adjustable straps, take up almost no storage space, and dramatically expand the exercise library available on the bar.

With rings, the client gains access to ring push-ups (which are significantly harder than floor press-ups due to the instability demand), ring rows (a superior version of the inverted row with adjustable difficulty), ring dips (one of the best tricep and chest exercises available without a bench), and eventually more advanced movements like ring muscle-ups and ring support holds. The instability of rings also recruits stabilising muscles that fixed-bar exercises do not reach, making them a genuine strength and muscle-building tool rather than just a novelty.

**What to buy:** Wooden gymnastic rings with adjustable nylon straps. Wood is preferred over plastic because it provides better grip, is more comfortable on the hands, and is more durable. The straps should be long enough to allow the rings to hang at various heights from the pull-up bar. Most sets come with straps of 4–5 metres, which is more than sufficient. Recommended brands include Pellor, Alpidex, and Gravity Fitness. A quality wooden ring set costs approximately £25–£40 and represents exceptional value given the exercise variety it unlocks.

---

## Tier 3 — Buy Third
### Estimated Cost: £100–£300 Total

These purchases are for when the client has been training consistently for six months or more, has genuinely outgrown the Tier 1 and Tier 2 equipment, and is ready to invest more seriously in his home setup.

### 5. Adjustable Weight Bench — £80–£150

A bench transforms dumbbell training. Without a bench, dumbbell pressing is limited to floor press variations, which restrict range of motion at the bottom of the movement. A bench allows full-range dumbbell bench press, incline press, single-arm dumbbell rows with proper support, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats with a more stable rear foot elevation than a sofa or chair provides.

**What to buy:** An **adjustable FID bench** — flat, incline, and decline positions. This is more versatile than a flat bench and does not cost significantly more. The bench must be rated for the loads the client will be using — check the weight capacity before purchasing. It should also fold flat for storage, which is essential in a small flat. Recommended options include the JLL FID bench, the Mirafit M100 adjustable bench, and the Marcy SB-261W. All fold for storage and are rated to 150kg or above. Budget approximately £80–£130 for a quality option.

### 6. Heavier Dumbbell Additions or Barbell — £100–£250

At some point, the adjustable dumbbells will reach their maximum weight and the client will need more load for compound movements like Romanian deadlifts and rows. There are two paths here depending on his space and ambitions.

**Path A — Heavier Adjustable Dumbbells:** If the flat remains the training space long-term, upgrading to a higher-capacity adjustable dumbbell set — such as the Bowflex SelectTech 1090, which adjusts to 41kg per dumbbell — is the most space-efficient solution. This costs approximately £300–£400 for the pair but eliminates the need for a barbell and plates entirely.

**Path B — Barbell and Weight Plates:** If the client has access to a slightly larger space — a garage, a spare room, or a garden — a standard Olympic barbell with a set of bumper plates is the most cost-effective way to add serious load. A 20kg Olympic barbell with 60–80kg of bumper plates costs approximately £150–£250 second-hand and opens up barbell deadlifts, rows, overhead press, and eventually squats if a rack is added later. This is the path toward a proper home gym and is only worth pursuing if the space genuinely supports it.

For a small flat, Path A is almost always the right recommendation.

---

## What Not to Buy

This is as important as the purchasing guide itself. The home fitness market is full of products that are heavily marketed, widely purchased, and largely useless. Save your client money by steering him away from the following.

**Treadmills and Exercise Bikes:** These are large, expensive, and redundant for someone following a structured cardio programme. They also break down, are difficult to dispose of, and dominate small spaces. The cardio programme in this plan requires no equipment whatsoever.

**Ab Rollers and Core Gadgets:** The hollow body holds, dead bugs, and plank variations in this programme are more effective core training tools than any ab roller or vibrating belt. These products exist to sell the idea of easy abs, not to produce them.

**Suspension Trainers (TRX):** These are not bad products — they are genuinely effective. However, gymnastic rings at a quarter of the price do everything a TRX does and more. There is no reason to buy both.

**Fixed-Weight Dumbbell Sets (Full Rack):** A full rack of fixed dumbbells from 2kg to 30kg takes up enormous space, costs several hundred pounds, and is completely unnecessary when adjustable options exist. The only exception is buying two or three specific fixed weights second-hand at low cost.

**Weighted Vests:** These are worth mentioning because they are genuinely useful for bodyweight training — adding load to press-ups, pull-ups, and squats without changing the movement pattern. However, they are a Tier 3 or Tier 4 purchase at best, and only relevant once the client has exhausted the progression options available through bands, dumbbells, and rings. A quality weighted vest costs £40–£80 and is worth considering eventually, but not before the higher-priority items above.

**Smith Machines and Cable Machines:** These are gym equipment designed for gym spaces. They are expensive, enormous, and entirely inappropriate for a small flat. If the client ever wants access to cable machines, a gym membership is a far more sensible solution than buying one.

---

## The Ideal Small Flat Home Gym — Final Picture

If the client follows this purchasing guide in order and invests sensibly over six to twelve months of consistent training, his eventual setup will look like this.

- Doorway pull-up bar — already owned
- Yoga mat — already owned
- Resistance band set (five bands) — £25–£35
- Heavy pull-up assistance band — £10–£15
- Adjustable dumbbells (2–24kg) — £90–£120
- 16kg kettlebell — £35–£50
- Wooden gymnastic rings — £25–£40
- Adjustable FID bench — £80–£130

**Total investment: approximately £265–£390** spread across six to twelve months of training.

This setup, in a space no larger than two metres by two metres, supports a training programme that the vast majority of commercial gym members could not match for effectiveness. It covers every major movement pattern, allows precise progressive overload, and will serve him for years without becoming obsolete.

The pull-up bar he already owns cost him perhaps £25. The programme built on it cost him nothing but effort. Everything else is just making a good thing better.

# Phase 2 Revised — Weeks 5–8: High Intensity Strength Development

---

## Revised Philosophy for Phase 2

The original Phase 2 was deliberately conservative, treating the upper/lower split as a stepping stone between foundation work and the peak phase. That changes now. Your client has four weeks of consistent training behind him, his movement patterns are established, his connective tissue has had time to adapt, and his nervous system is primed for a genuine challenge. 

The revised Phase 2 operates on a simple principle: **every session should feel hard**. Not recklessly hard — technique still governs everything — but hard in the way that produces real adaptation. The client should finish upper sessions with his chest, back, and arms genuinely fatigued, and finish lower sessions with his legs feeling like they have been worked rather than merely exercised.

To achieve this, the revised Phase 2 introduces five intensity techniques that were absent from the original plan.

---

## The Five Intensity Techniques

Understanding these techniques matters because they are the engine of the revised phase. Each one is a specific tool for making bodyweight training harder without adding external load.

### Technique 1: Mechanical Drop Sets

A mechanical drop set moves through a sequence of exercises from hardest to easiest within the same movement pattern, performing each to near-failure before immediately transitioning to the easier variation without rest. This allows the muscle to continue working past the point where it would otherwise fail on the harder exercise.

For pressing, the sequence runs: **Decline Press-Up → Standard Press-Up → Incline Press-Up**. The client performs as many decline press-ups as possible with good form, immediately drops to standard press-ups and continues, then immediately drops to incline press-ups and continues. That entire sequence counts as one set. Rest, then repeat.

For pulling, the sequence runs: **Chin-Up or Negative → Inverted Row (horizontal) → Inverted Row (45 degrees)**. Same principle — hardest to easiest, no rest between variations.

### Technique 2: Paused Reps

A paused rep involves holding the most mechanically disadvantaged position of an exercise — typically the bottom — for a prescribed count before completing the rep. This eliminates the stretch reflex, which is the elastic energy stored in a muscle at the end of the eccentric phase that normally assists the concentric phase. Removing this assistance forces the muscle to generate force from a dead stop, which is significantly harder and produces greater strength adaptation.

A paused squat holds at the bottom for two seconds. A paused press-up holds chest-to-floor for two seconds. A paused chin-up holds at the top with chin over bar for two seconds. The prescribed pause duration will be noted in each session.

### Technique 3: Density Blocks

A density block prescribes a fixed time window — typically eight to twelve minutes — and a specific exercise or pair of exercises. The client performs as many quality reps as possible within that window, resting only as needed to maintain form. The goal each week is to accumulate more total reps in the same time window. This is one of the most effective methods for driving volume progression in bodyweight training because it makes progress visible and competitive — the client is always racing his previous score.

### Technique 4: Rest-Pause Sets

A rest-pause set takes a single set and extends it beyond the point of initial failure using brief intra-set rest periods. The client performs reps to near-failure, rests for fifteen seconds, performs more reps to near-failure, rests for fifteen seconds, and performs a final cluster. All three clusters count as one set. This technique is particularly effective for pull-up development because it allows significantly more total pull-up volume per session than straight sets alone.

### Technique 5: Tempo Contrast

Tempo contrast pairs a slow eccentric with an explosive concentric within the same set. The client lowers for four seconds, pauses for one second, then drives up as fast as possible. The slow eccentric builds strength and control through the full range of motion. The explosive concentric recruits fast-twitch muscle fibres that slower tempos do not access. Together they produce a more complete strength stimulus than either approach alone.

## The Purpose of Saturday

Before writing a single exercise, it is worth being clear about what Saturday is and what it is not. Saturday is not a fourth strength session. It is not a cardio session with a different name. It is not an opportunity to squeeze more volume into the week under the guise of fun.

Saturday is a **play day**. It exists because sustainable long-term training requires the client to associate exercise with enjoyment as well as results. The research on exercise adherence is unambiguous on this point — people who find training fun are dramatically more likely to still be training in five years than people who treat every session as a grind. Building one session per week that the client genuinely looks forward to is not a soft addition to a serious programme. It is a serious addition to a serious programme.

With that said, Saturday sessions are designed with a secondary eye on physical development. They will improve conditioning, coordination, power, and mental toughness without the client feeling like he is being trained. The best finisher sessions feel like games. The adaptation they produce is real.

**Saturday sessions run 25–35 minutes maximum.** They begin with a brief movement warm-up and end with a specific cool-down. Everything in between should feel different from the Monday-Wednesday-Friday structure — faster, more varied, more spontaneous, and occasionally slightly ridiculous. That is the point.

**One important rule:** If the client is genuinely fatigued from the week's training — not just mildly tired, but actually run down — Saturday becomes a rest day. Fun training on a depleted body stops being fun very quickly and risks the kind of accumulated fatigue that derails the main programme. Give him permission to skip Saturday without guilt when his body needs it.

---

## Saturday Session Format

Every Saturday session follows the same three-part structure regardless of the specific content.

**Part 1 — Movement Warm-Up (5 minutes)**
A consistent, brief warm-up that prepares the body for varied movement without being so long that it eats into the fun portion of the session.

**Part 2 — The Main Event (20–25 minutes)**
The specific challenge, game, or circuit for that week. This changes every week and is the part the client should be looking forward to.

**Part 3 — Cool-Down and Reflection (5 minutes)**
Light movement, breathing, and a moment to acknowledge what was just accomplished. This is also where the client records his score, time, or result for the week — because tracking progress is motivating even when the session is supposed to be fun.
