## Phase 1 Saturday Sessions — Weeks 1–4
### Theme: Skill and Exploration

Phase 1 Saturday sessions focus on movement exploration and skill development. The client is new to structured training and his body is still learning how to move well. Saturday sessions in this phase introduce movement patterns in a low-pressure, playful context that reinforces what is being built in the main sessions without adding significant fatigue.

### Week 1 Saturday — The Deck of Cards

This is one of the oldest and most enjoyable bodyweight training games in existence. It requires nothing but a standard deck of playing cards and a willingness to commit to whatever comes up.

**Setup:** Assign an exercise to each suit.

- Hearts — Press-Up
- Diamonds — Bodyweight Squat
- Clubs — Glute Bridge
- Spades — Mountain Climber (each knee drive counts as one rep)

Shuffle the deck. Flip cards one at a time. The number on the card is the number of reps to perform of the corresponding exercise. Face cards count as ten reps. Aces count as eleven reps. Jokers — if included — are a wildcard: thirty seconds of the client's choice of any exercise performed as fast as possible.

**How to play:** Flip a card, perform the reps immediately, flip the next card. Rest only when genuinely needed. The goal is to get through as many cards as possible in twenty minutes. Record how many cards were completed. Next time the game is played, beat that number.

The beauty of this format is that the randomness removes the psychological weight of a prescribed workout. The client is not thinking about sets and reps — he is just responding to the next card. Twenty minutes passes surprisingly quickly.

**What to tell the client:** Do not count this as a workout. Count it as a game you happen to sweat during.

---

### Week 2 Saturday — The Ladder Challenge

Ladders are a simple and deeply satisfying training format. The client climbs up a rep ladder and then climbs back down, with the total volume accumulating naturally as the session progresses.

**The Ladder:**

Perform the following sequence, starting at one rep of each exercise and adding one rep each round until reaching ten, then descending back to one.

- Press-Up
- Bodyweight Squat
- Dead Bug (each side)

Round 1: 1 press-up, 1 squat, 1 dead bug each side
Round 2: 2 press-ups, 2 squats, 2 dead bugs each side
Round 3: 3 of each
...continue to Round 10...
Round 11: 9 of each (descending)
...continue back to Round 20: 1 of each

Rest as needed between rounds but try to keep rest periods short — the ladder format naturally manages intensity because early rounds are easy and later rounds are hard.

**The Score:** Record the time taken to complete the full ladder from 1 to 10 and back to 1. This is the benchmark. If the client does not finish in the available time, record how far he got.

**Total volume if completed:** 100 press-ups, 100 squats, 100 dead bugs each side. This sounds enormous but the ladder format distributes the volume in a way that makes it surprisingly manageable.

---

### Week 3 Saturday — The Movement Flow

This session is deliberately different from everything else in the programme. It is slow, exploratory, and focused on body awareness rather than performance. Think of it as movement meditation.

**The Flow:**

The client spends twenty minutes moving continuously through the following sequence, holding each position for as long as feels natural before transitioning to the next. There is no prescribed time for each position — the client listens to his body and moves when he feels ready. The sequence repeats for the full twenty minutes.

- Standing — reach arms overhead, take three deep breaths
- Forward fold — hang from the hips, let the head drop, bend knees slightly if needed
- Squat — sit into a deep bodyweight squat, use hands on floor for balance if needed
- Kneeling — transition to kneeling, sit back on heels
- Child's pose — arms extended, forehead on mat
- Cat-cow — ten slow repetitions
- Downward dog — hold for five breaths
- Plank — hold for ten seconds
- Press-up position — lower slowly to the floor
- Cobra — press chest up, look forward
- Roll to seated — cross-legged
- Spinal twist — right, then left
- Stand — return to the top

Play ambient music or nature sounds. No timer, no counting, no performance metric. The only instruction is to move slowly and breathe deliberately.

**What to tell the client:** This session will feel strange if he is used to thinking of exercise as effort. Tell him that the ability to move well through a full range of motion is a genuine physical quality, and this session is training it. His joints, his nervous system, and his sleep quality will all benefit.

---

### Week 4 Saturday — Deload Week Fun Session

Week 4 is a deload week, so Saturday is deliberately light. This session should feel like active play rather than training in any meaningful sense.

**The Animal Movement Session**

The client spends twenty minutes moving around the mat space using animal locomotion patterns. These look ridiculous. They are also genuinely effective for developing coordination, shoulder stability, hip mobility, and core control — and they are fun in a way that almost nothing else in a training programme is.

- **Bear crawl** — on hands and feet (not knees), crawl forward and backward across the mat. Keep hips low and move opposite hand and foot simultaneously.
- **Crab walk** — seated position, hands and feet on floor, hips lifted, walk sideways and forward.
- **Inchworm walk** — hinge at hips, walk hands out to plank, walk feet back to hands, repeat across the mat.
- **Frog jump** — squat deep, place hands on floor, jump feet forward to hands, repeat.
- **Lizard crawl** — in a low press-up position, bring one foot forward to the outside of the same-side hand, alternate sides as you crawl forward.

Spend three to four minutes on each movement, transitioning between them freely. No performance metric, no score. Just move.

## Phase 2 Saturday Sessions — Weeks 5–8
### Theme: Competition and Challenge

### Week 5 Saturday — The 10-Minute AMRAP Gauntlet

AMRAP stands for As Many Rounds As Possible. It is one of the most effective and enjoyable training formats available because the open-ended nature — there is no prescribed number of rounds, just a time limit — removes the psychological ceiling of a fixed workout. The client always has the option to push harder.

**The Circuit:**

- Press-Up — 5 reps
- Bodyweight Squat — 10 reps
- Mountain Climber — 10 reps each leg
- Glute Bridge — 10 reps
- Dead Bug — 5 reps each side

Set a timer for ten minutes. Perform as many complete rounds of the circuit as possible. Record the number of complete rounds plus any additional reps completed in the final partial round. This is the score.

Rest only when genuinely needed. The rep counts are deliberately low per exercise so that transitions between exercises are the primary rest.

**The Score System:** Write the score down somewhere visible — on his phone, on a whiteboard, on a sticky note on the fridge. This number matters. Every time this format appears in the programme, the goal is to beat the previous score.

### Week 6 Saturday — The Pull-Up Bar Challenge

This session is entirely focused on the pull-up bar and is designed to feel like a personal challenge rather than a training session. It works particularly well at this point in the programme because the client has been building pulling strength for five weeks and is ready to see what he can actually do.

**The Challenge — Three Tests:**

**Test 1: Maximum Dead Hang**
The client hangs from the bar with an overhand grip and holds for as long as possible. Record the time. This tests grip strength and shoulder stability. A beginner target is 60 seconds — if he beats this, it is a genuine achievement worth acknowledging.

Rest three minutes.

**Test 2: Maximum Pull-Up or Chin-Up Reps**
One set, maximum effort, full range of motion. Record the number. If he cannot perform a full pull-up, record the number of negatives performed with a five-second lowering phase before form breaks down.

Rest three minutes.

**Test 3: The Accumulation Challenge**
The client must accumulate twenty total pull-up or chin-up reps — or forty total negative reps — in as few sets as possible, resting as needed between sets. Record the number of sets required. The goal over subsequent weeks is to achieve the same total volume in fewer sets, which represents genuine strength endurance improvement.

**After the three tests:** Ten minutes of free movement — shadow boxing, animal locomotion, or the movement flow from week three. Whatever feels good. The tests are the session. Everything after is just enjoyment.

---

### Week 7 Saturday — The Benchmark Circuit

This session introduces a specific benchmark circuit that will be repeated in week twelve as a final performance test. The client performs it for the first time this week without any expectation of a particular score — the week seven result is simply the baseline.

**The Benchmark — The Home Athlete Test:**

Perform the following circuit for time. Complete all reps of each exercise before moving to the next. Rest as needed but the clock keeps running.

- Press-Up — 20 reps
- Bodyweight Squat — 30 reps
- Pull-Up or Chin-Up (or 10 negatives if full reps not yet available) — 10 reps
- Mountain Climber — 20 reps each leg
- Bulgarian Split Squat — 15 reps each leg
- Pike Press-Up — 15 reps
- Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 20 reps each leg
- Dead Bug — 10 reps each side
- Inverted Row — 15 reps
- Hollow Body Hold — 30 seconds

Record the total time. This is the week seven benchmark. When this circuit reappears in week twelve, the goal is to beat this time by a meaningful margin. Five weeks of hard training should produce a noticeable improvement.

**What to tell the client:** Do not pace this. Go as hard as he can from the first exercise. The time is only meaningful if it represents a genuine maximum effort.

---

### Week 8 Saturday — Deload Week Play Session

Week 8 is another deload week. Saturday is light and genuinely playful.

**The Skill Session — Learning Something New**

Spend twenty minutes attempting one of the following bodyweight skills. These are not exercises in the traditional sense — they are movement skills that take time to develop and provide a completely different kind of satisfaction from standard training.

**Option A — The Crow Pose (Bakasana)**
A yoga balance pose where the client balances on his hands with knees resting on the backs of his upper arms. This requires wrist strength, core tension, and the willingness to fall forward slightly. Most people can achieve a brief hold within one or two sessions of practice. It looks impressive and feels genuinely satisfying to nail.

**How to practice:** Start in a deep squat with hands on the floor shoulder-width apart. Place knees on the backs of the upper arms as high as possible. Lean forward slowly, shifting weight onto the hands, until the feet lift off the floor. Hold for as long as possible. Fall forward onto a pillow or folded mat if needed — this removes the fear of falling and accelerates learning.

**Option B — The L-Sit Progression**
Sitting on the floor with legs extended, place hands beside the hips and press down to lift the hips off the floor. The goal is eventually to hold the body in an L-shape with legs parallel to the floor. This is a serious core and tricep strength challenge that most people cannot achieve immediately — but the progression toward it is valuable training in itself.

**How to practice:** Start with bent knees, lifting just the hips. Progress to one leg extended, then both. Hold each progression for as long as possible and record the best hold time.

**Option C — The Handstand Progression Against the Wall**
Kick up into a handstand against the wall and hold for as long as possible. This develops shoulder strength, body awareness, and the kind of inverted balance that transfers surprisingly well to pressing strength.

**How to practice:** Place hands on the floor approximately thirty centimetres from the wall. Kick one leg up and follow with the other until both feet rest against the wall. Hold, focusing on straight arms, engaged core, and pushing the floor away. Record the hold time.

Spend the full twenty minutes practicing whichever skill appeals most. Progress will feel slow — that is normal and expected. The point is exploration, not mastery.

## Phase 3 Saturday Sessions — Weeks 9–12
### Theme: Performance and Celebration

Phase 3 Saturday sessions reflect the peak intensity of the main programme. They are the most demanding Saturday sessions of the twelve weeks but retain the fun, game-like quality that defines the day. They also build toward the week twelve finale, which is the most satisfying session of the entire programme.

---

### Week 9 Saturday — The Pyramid of Pain

The pyramid format from week two returns but significantly harder. This is not a gentle ladder — it is a genuine physical challenge that will test everything the client has built over the previous eight weeks.

**The Pyramid:**

Climb from one to seven and back down to one. No rest between exercises within a round. Rest thirty seconds between rounds.

- Chin-Up or Negative — reps as prescribed per round
- Decline Press-Up — reps as prescribed per round
- Bulgarian Split Squat each leg — reps as prescribed per round
- Mountain Climber each leg — reps as prescribed per round

Round 1: 1 rep of each
Round 2: 2 reps of each
Round 3: 3 reps of each
Round 4: 4 reps of each
Round 5: 5 reps of each
Round 6: 6 reps of each
Round 7: 7 reps of each
Round 8: 6 reps of each (descending)
...continue back to Round 14: 1 rep of each

**The Score:** Time to complete the full pyramid. If the client cannot complete the full pyramid in the available time, record how far he got.

**Total volume if completed:** 49 chin-ups or negatives, 49 decline press-ups, 49 Bulgarian split squats each leg, 49 mountain climbers each leg. This is a serious amount of work disguised as a counting game.

---

### Week 10 Saturday — The Gauntlet

The gauntlet is a format where the client moves through a series of individual challenges back to back, with each challenge having a specific target. The goal is to complete every challenge successfully. Failing a challenge means repeating it before moving on.

**The Challenges:**

**Challenge 1 — The Press-Up Hold**
Hold the bottom position of a press-up — chest one centimetre from the floor, body rigid — for thirty seconds without touching the floor. If he touches the floor, rest ten seconds and repeat. Move on only when the thirty seconds is achieved.

**Challenge 2 — The Squat Sit**
Sit in a deep bodyweight squat — heels flat on the floor if possible, or elevated on a folded mat if not — for two minutes continuously. If he stands up, rest ten seconds and continue the clock from where he left off. The two minutes must be accumulated without standing.

**Challenge 3 — The Pull-Up Bar Hold**
Hang from the pull-up bar at the top of a chin-up position — chin over bar, elbows bent — for as long as possible. Target is twenty seconds. If he cannot hold for twenty seconds, rest thirty seconds and try again. Move on only when twenty seconds is achieved.

**Challenge 4 — The Mountain Climber Century**
Perform one hundred mountain climbers — fifty each leg — as fast as possible without stopping. If he stops, he continues from where he left off but the clock keeps running. Record the total time.

**Challenge 5 — The Nordic Curl Gauntlet**
Perform five Nordic curl negatives — lowering as slowly as possible each time — with no more than thirty seconds rest between reps. If he rushes the lowering phase, the rep does not count.

**Challenge 6 — The Final Hang**
End the gauntlet with a maximum effort dead hang. Whatever he has left, he gives to this hang. Record the time.

**The Score:** Total time to complete all six challenges. The client should feel genuinely accomplished when he finishes this session.

---

### Week 11 Saturday — The Team Challenge (Solo Version)

This session is designed around the concept of a team workout performed solo — the client works through a series of tasks that would typically be shared between multiple people, completing everything himself. It sounds simple but the psychological effect of framing a solo session as a team effort is surprisingly powerful.

**The Mission:**

The client must complete the following total rep targets. He can break them up any way he chooses — any set size, any order, any rest period. The only rule is that every rep must be completed before the session ends.

- 100 Press-Ups (any variation)
- 100 Bodyweight Squats
- 50 Pull-Ups or Chin-Ups (or 100 negatives)
- 100 Mountain Climbers each leg
- 50 Pike Press-Ups
- 100 Glute Bridges
- 50 Dead Bugs each side

**The Strategy Element:** The client decides how to approach this. Does he do large sets early and small sets when fatigued? Does he alternate between upper and lower body exercises to manage fatigue? Does he tackle the hardest exercise first or save it for last? This decision-making element makes the session feel genuinely engaging rather than mechanical.

**The Score:** Total time to complete all reps. This is a long session — it may take thirty to forty minutes depending on fitness level. That is acceptable for week eleven. The client should be proud of completing it regardless of time.

---

### Week 12 Saturday — The Grand Finale

The final Saturday session of the programme is the most important one. It has two parts: the benchmark retest and the celebration.

**Part 1 — The Home Athlete Test Retest**

Repeat the benchmark circuit from week seven exactly. Same exercises, same rep counts, same format. The client goes as hard as he can from the first rep.

- Press-Up — 20 reps
- Bodyweight Squat — 30 reps
- Pull-Up or Chin-Up — 10 reps (or negatives)
- Mountain Climber — 20 reps each leg
- Bulgarian Split Squat — 15 reps each leg
- Pike Press-Up — 15 reps
- Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 20 reps each leg
- Dead Bug — 10 reps each side
- Inverted Row — 15 reps
- Hollow Body Hold — 30 seconds

Record the time. Compare to week seven. The improvement — and there will be improvement — is twelve weeks of consistent work made visible in a single number. This moment is worth acknowledging properly.

**Part 2 — The Skill Showcase**

After a ten-minute rest following the benchmark retest, the client returns to whichever skill he practiced in week eight — crow pose, L-sit, or handstand — and performs his best attempt. He has had four weeks of additional strength development since week eight. The improvement in skill performance will often surprise him.

**Part 3 — The Cool-Down Reflection**

The final cool-down of the programme is extended to ten minutes. During this cool-down, encourage the client to think about three specific things.

First, where he started. Week one, session one — the incline press-ups, the twenty-second dead hangs, the twenty-minute LISS walks that felt like a genuine effort. Second, where he is now. The pull-ups, the Nordic curls, the Bulgarian split squats, the benchmark circuit time. Third, where he wants to go. The programme ends here but the training does not. What does week thirteen look like? What equipment is he going to buy first? What is the next goal?

**What to tell the client at the end of week twelve:** The programme is finished. The habit is not. Everything built over these twelve weeks — the strength, the fitness, the nutritional awareness, the Saturday ritual of doing something physical that feels good — belongs to him now. The equipment will come. The goals will evolve. But the most important thing he built over these twelve weeks was not his press-up numbers or his pull-up reps. It was the identity of someone who trains. That identity is worth more than any programme.

# Mobility Programme
### Integrated with 12-Week Home Strength Programme

---

## Why Mobility Matters for This Client Specifically

Before writing a single stretch, it is worth being direct about why mobility deserves its own dedicated section in this programme rather than a few token stretches bolted onto the end of sessions.

Your client is 27, sedentary enough to be classified as a beginner, and almost certainly spending a significant portion of his day sitting. The modern sitting lifestyle produces a remarkably consistent pattern of dysfunction that shows up in virtually every beginner who walks — or in this case, logs on — to start training. Hip flexors are shortened and overactive. Thoracic spine is stiff and rounded forward. Glutes are inhibited. Shoulder internal rotators are tight while external rotators are weak. Ankle dorsiflexion is restricted. This pattern does not just limit performance — it actively works against the training programme by reducing range of motion in squats, limiting overhead position in pike press-ups, restricting scapular movement in pull-ups, and increasing injury risk across every movement pattern.

Mobility work in this programme therefore serves three distinct functions. It corrects the postural and movement restrictions that sitting creates. It enhances performance in the strength sessions by allowing fuller, safer ranges of motion. And it accelerates recovery by promoting blood flow, reducing neural tension, and improving the quality of movement patterns between sessions.

The mobility programme is structured as **three distinct routines** that serve different purposes and are performed at different times. Understanding when to use each routine is as important as knowing the routines themselves.

---

## The Three Routines

**Routine 1 — The Morning Wake-Up (8–10 minutes)**
Performed every morning, seven days a week, immediately upon waking. This routine addresses the stiffness that accumulates overnight, activates the muscles that sitting will inhibit throughout the day, and sets a positive physical tone for the morning. It is performed on the yoga mat in whatever the client sleeps in. No warm-up required because the routine itself is the warm-up.

**Routine 2 — The Pre-Session Primer (8–10 minutes)**
Performed immediately before every strength, cardio, or Saturday session. This routine replaces the generic warm-ups described in earlier sections of the programme — it is more targeted, more effective, and more directly relevant to the movement patterns about to be trained. It is dynamic rather than static, meaning it moves through ranges of motion rather than holding positions.

**Routine 3 — The Evening Wind-Down (12–15 minutes)**
Performed on three to four evenings per week, ideally on training days before sleep. This routine uses longer static holds and parasympathetic nervous system activation to promote recovery, improve flexibility over time, and improve sleep quality. It is the most important routine for long-term mobility development because the longer holds — two to three minutes per position — are what actually change tissue length and joint range of motion over weeks and months.

---

## Key Mobility Areas

The programme targets seven specific areas that are most commonly restricted in a sedentary 27-year-old male and most directly relevant to the exercises in this programme.

**Hip Flexors** — Shortened by sitting, they limit hip extension in lunges and split squats, cause anterior pelvic tilt that stresses the lower back, and inhibit glute activation.

**Thoracic Spine** — Stiffened by forward head posture and rounded shoulders, it limits overhead reach in pike press-ups, restricts scapular movement in pull-ups and rows, and contributes to shoulder impingement.

**Shoulders and Chest** — Tightened by internal rotation from keyboard and phone use, they limit the bottom position of press-ups, restrict the overhead position, and reduce pulling range of motion.

**Hamstrings** — Shortened by sitting, they limit hip hinge depth, contribute to posterior pelvic tilt in squats, and increase lower back stress.

**Ankles** — Restricted dorsiflexion limits squat depth, forces compensatory forward lean, and increases knee stress during lunges and split squats.

**Glutes and Piriformis** — Tightened by sitting and inhibited by hip flexor dominance, they limit hip internal rotation and contribute to knee tracking issues in squats.

**Lats and Thoracolumbar Fascia** — Tightened by pull-up training and sitting, they limit overhead reach and contribute to lower back stiffness.

---

## How to Perform Mobility Work Effectively

Three principles govern every mobility session in this programme.

**Breathe into the restriction.** When the client reaches a position of tension, the instinct is to hold the breath. This is counterproductive — breath holding increases neural tension and prevents the nervous system from allowing greater range of motion. Every hold should involve deliberate, slow exhalation into the point of restriction. The position should deepen slightly with each exhale.

**Never force range of motion.** Mobility work should produce a sensation of productive tension — a deep stretch that is uncomfortable in a satisfying way. It should never produce sharp, shooting, or joint pain. If the client reports pain rather than tension, the position needs to be modified or the exercise replaced.

**Consistency beats intensity.** Ten minutes of mobility work every day produces dramatically better results than sixty minutes once a week. The nervous system adapts to positions it visits regularly. Infrequent long sessions teach the body that a position is a rare event. Daily shorter sessions teach the body that the position is normal. Normal positions become accessible positions.

# Routine 1 — The Morning Wake-Up

**Duration:** 8–10 minutes
**When:** Every morning, seven days a week, immediately upon waking
**Equipment:** Yoga mat
**Format:** Flow-based, moving continuously through positions with brief holds

---

## The Sequence

### 1. Supine Knee Hug — 30 seconds each leg, then both legs together

Lie on the back on the mat. Draw one knee toward the chest and hold it there with both hands, feeling the gentle traction in the lower back and hip. Breathe slowly. After thirty seconds, switch legs. After both individual legs, draw both knees to the chest simultaneously and rock gently side to side for fifteen seconds. This decompresses the lumbar spine after a night of relative immobility and is the ideal way to begin every morning.

### 2. Supine Spinal Twist — 45 seconds each side

From lying on the back, draw the right knee to the chest, then let it fall across the body to the left while extending the right arm out to the right side. The left hand rests lightly on the outside of the right knee. Look to the right. Breathe deeply, allowing the thoracic spine to rotate with each exhale. After forty-five seconds, return to centre and repeat on the other side. This addresses thoracic rotation restriction and the lower back stiffness that accumulates overnight.

### 3. Cat-Cow — 10 slow repetitions

Come to hands and knees on the mat, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. On the inhale, drop the belly toward the floor, lift the chest and tailbone — this is cow. On the exhale, round the spine toward the ceiling, tuck the chin and tailbone — this is cat. Move slowly and deliberately, spending two to three seconds at each end of the range. This is not a warm-up exercise performed quickly — it is a spinal mobility exercise performed with full attention to each vertebral segment moving in sequence.

### 4. Thread the Needle — 30 seconds each side

From hands and knees, slide the right arm along the floor under the left arm, allowing the right shoulder and ear to rest on the mat. The left arm can remain extended or press into the floor to deepen the rotation. This targets thoracic rotation and posterior shoulder tightness — two of the most common restrictions in desk workers. After thirty seconds, press back to hands and knees and repeat on the other side.

### 5. Child's Pose with Lateral Reach — 30 seconds centre, 20 seconds each side

From hands and knees, sit the hips back toward the heels and extend the arms forward on the mat. Hold the central position for thirty seconds, breathing into the lower back and feeling the lats lengthen. Then walk both hands to the right, creating a lateral stretch through the left side of the torso and left lat. Hold twenty seconds. Return to centre and walk hands to the left. Hold twenty seconds. This addresses lat tightness that develops from pull-up training and general sitting posture.

### 6. Hip Flexor Kneeling Stretch — 45 seconds each side

From kneeling, step the right foot forward into a half-kneeling position — right knee at ninety degrees, left knee on the mat. Shift the hips forward gently until a stretch is felt in the front of the left hip. Keep the torso upright — do not lean forward, which reduces the hip flexor stretch. For a deeper stretch, raise the left arm overhead and lean slightly to the right. Breathe into the front of the hip. After forty-five seconds, switch sides. This is the single most important mobility exercise for a sedentary client and should be performed with full attention every morning.

### 7. Seated Hamstring Reach — 30 seconds each leg

Sit on the mat with both legs extended. Flex the right foot and reach both hands toward the right foot, hinging from the hips rather than rounding the lower back. The goal is not to touch the toes — it is to feel the hamstring lengthen while the spine remains relatively neutral. Hold thirty seconds, breathing into the back of the thigh. Switch legs. If hamstring tightness is severe, bend the knee slightly to allow a neutral spine position.

### 8. Ankle Circles and Dorsiflexion — 30 seconds each ankle

Sit on the mat with legs extended. Rotate the right ankle in large, slow circles — ten clockwise, ten counterclockwise. Then flex and point the foot ten times, emphasising the dorsiflexion — pulling the toes toward the shin — as much as possible. Switch ankles. This addresses the ankle restriction that limits squat depth and is particularly important on lower body training days.

### 9. Standing Thoracic Extension — 10 repetitions

Stand facing a wall, approximately one arm's length away. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height. Walk the feet back slightly and hinge at the hips until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor and the arms are extended. From this position, let the chest drop toward the floor, creating extension through the thoracic spine. Hold the bottom position for two seconds, then return to neutral. Repeat ten times. This is one of the most effective thoracic mobility exercises available and directly improves overhead position for pike press-ups and pull-up bar work.

### 10. Three Deep Breaths Standing

Stand tall, feet hip-width apart. Take three slow, deliberate breaths — inhale for four counts through the nose, hold for two counts, exhale for six counts through the mouth. On each exhale, consciously relax the shoulders away from the ears. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system, sets a calm and focused tone for the day, and reinforces the breathing habits that will serve the client in training sessions.

# Routine 2 — The Pre-Session Primer

**Duration:** 8–10 minutes
**When:** Immediately before every training session — strength, cardio, or Saturday
**Equipment:** Yoga mat, pull-up bar for one exercise
**Format:** Dynamic — moving through ranges of motion rather than holding static positions

This routine replaces all warm-ups described in previous sections of the programme. It is more targeted and more effective than the generic warm-ups previously prescribed. The dynamic nature of the exercises — moving through range rather than holding — is appropriate pre-training because it increases tissue temperature, activates the nervous system, and rehearses movement patterns without the neural inhibition that prolonged static stretching can cause immediately before training.

---

## The Sequence

### 1. Inchworm with Press-Up — 6 repetitions

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips and place both hands on the floor. Walk the hands forward until in a full press-up position. Perform one press-up. Walk the feet toward the hands. Stand. Repeat six times. This single exercise warms up the hamstrings, shoulders, chest, core, and wrists simultaneously and is one of the most efficient movement preparation exercises available.

### 2. World's Greatest Stretch — 5 repetitions each side

Step the right foot forward into a lunge position. Place the right hand on the floor inside the right foot. Rotate the right arm toward the ceiling, following the hand with the eyes. Return the hand to the floor. Shift the hips back slightly to straighten the right leg and feel the hamstring stretch. Return to the lunge. That is one repetition. Perform five on the right side, then five on the left. This exercise earns its name — it addresses hip flexors, thoracic rotation, hamstrings, and groin in a single flowing movement.

### 3. Hip Circle in Deep Squat — 10 circles each direction

Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly. Squat as deep as possible, using hands on the floor or holding a doorframe for balance if needed. From the bottom of the squat, make large circles with the hips — rotating the pelvis clockwise for ten repetitions, then counterclockwise for ten. This mobilises the hip joint through its full range of motion and directly prepares the client for squat and lunge patterns.

### 4. Thoracic Rotation in Quadruped — 10 repetitions each side

Come to hands and knees. Place the right hand behind the head. Rotate the right elbow toward the left elbow, then open it toward the ceiling as far as possible. Follow the elbow with the eyes. Repeat ten times on the right, then ten on the left. This is a dynamic version of the thread-the-needle from the morning routine and directly prepares the thoracic spine for the rotation demands of pressing and pulling.

### 5. Leg Swing — 15 repetitions each direction each leg

Stand beside a wall, right hand on the wall for balance. Swing the left leg forward and back in a controlled arc, gradually increasing the range of motion over the fifteen repetitions. Then turn to face the wall and swing the left leg side to side. Repeat on the right leg. This dynamically mobilises the hip joint and activates the hip flexors and glutes before lower body training.

### 6. Scapular Wall Slide — 10 repetitions

Stand with the back against a wall, feet approximately fifteen centimetres from the baseboard. Press the lower back, upper back, and head against the wall. Raise the arms to a ninety-degree position — elbows bent, upper arms parallel to the floor — and press the backs of the hands and forearms against the wall. Slide the arms upward toward full overhead extension while maintaining contact between the arms and the wall. Return to the starting position. This is one of the most effective exercises for activating the lower trapezius and serratus anterior — the muscles responsible for healthy scapular movement in pull-ups and pressing. Perform ten slow repetitions before every session.

### 7. Ankle Dorsiflexion Mobilisation — 10 repetitions each ankle

Stand facing a wall, right foot approximately ten centimetres from the baseboard. Drive the right knee forward toward the wall, keeping the heel flat on the floor. The goal is to touch the knee to the wall while the heel remains down. If the knee cannot reach the wall, move the foot closer. If it can, move the foot further away. Ten repetitions each ankle. This directly addresses the ankle restriction that limits squat depth and is particularly important before lower body sessions.

### 8. Arm Circle Progression — 10 repetitions each direction

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Begin with small arm circles, gradually increasing the diameter over ten repetitions until performing the largest possible circles. Reverse direction for ten repetitions. This warms up the shoulder joint through its full range of motion and is particularly important before upper body sessions.

### 9. Jumping Jack or Step Jack — 30 seconds

Finish the primer with thirty seconds of jumping jacks — or step jacks if noise is a concern — to elevate heart rate and body temperature before the session begins. The client should feel warm and ready to train by the end of this exercise.

# Routine 3 — The Evening Wind-Down

**Duration:** 12–15 minutes
**When:** Three to four evenings per week, ideally on training days, performed thirty to sixty minutes before sleep
**Equipment:** Yoga mat, wall space
**Format:** Static holds of two to three minutes per position — this is what produces lasting flexibility change

This is the most important routine for long-term mobility development. The holds are long by conventional stretching standards — two to three minutes per position rather than the typical twenty to thirty seconds. This duration is necessary because meaningful change in tissue length and joint range of motion requires sustained time under tension. Short holds maintain existing range of motion. Long holds expand it.

The client should perform this routine in dim lighting with calm music or silence. The parasympathetic activation it produces — the shift from sympathetic fight-or-flight to rest-and-digest — directly improves sleep quality, which in turn directly improves recovery and training adaptation. This routine is therefore simultaneously a mobility tool and a sleep optimisation tool.

---

## The Sequence

### 1. Legs Up the Wall — 3 minutes

Lie on the back with the hips close to a wall and both legs extended up the wall. The legs can be straight or slightly bent depending on hamstring flexibility. Arms rest by the sides, palms facing up. Close the eyes and breathe slowly. This position reverses the effects of prolonged standing or sitting, reduces lower limb swelling, calms the nervous system, and gently stretches the hamstrings without any active effort. It is the ideal way to begin the evening routine because it immediately signals to the nervous system that the day's physical demands are over.

After three minutes, slowly lower the legs and transition to the next position without rushing.

### 2. Supine Figure-Four Hip Stretch — 2 minutes each side

Lie on the back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Cross the right ankle over the left thigh, just above the knee. Flex the right foot. Either stay here if the stretch is already intense, or draw the left knee toward the chest, threading the right hand through the gap between the legs to clasp the left shin or thigh. Hold for two full minutes, breathing slowly and allowing the right hip to relax with each exhale. This targets the piriformis and deep hip rotators — muscles that are chronically tight in people who sit and that directly affect squat mechanics and lower back comfort. Switch sides.

### 3. Couch Stretch — 2 minutes each side

This is the most effective hip flexor stretch available and is significantly more powerful than the standard kneeling hip flexor stretch. Kneel facing away from the sofa or wall. Place the right shin up the sofa or wall — the top of the foot rests against the sofa back or wall, the knee is on the floor or on a folded mat for padding. Step the left foot forward into a lunge position. Keeping the torso upright, shift the hips forward and down. The stretch in the front of the right hip should be intense. Hold for two full minutes, breathing into the hip flexor. Switch sides.

If the full position is too intense initially, begin with the shin on the floor rather than elevated — a standard kneeling hip flexor stretch — and progress to the elevated version over subsequent weeks as flexibility improves.

### 4. Doorframe Chest Stretch — 90 seconds each side

Stand in a doorframe. Place the right forearm against the doorframe with the elbow at shoulder height and the upper arm parallel to the floor. Step the right foot forward through the doorframe and rotate the body to the left until a stretch is felt across the right chest and front of the right shoulder. Hold for ninety seconds, breathing into the chest. This addresses the internal rotation tightness that develops from keyboard use and is directly relevant to press-up range of motion and shoulder health in pull-ups. Switch sides.

### 5. Thoracic Extension Over Rolled Mat — 2 minutes

Roll the yoga mat into a firm cylinder approximately ten centimetres in diameter. Place it on the floor perpendicular to the body. Sit in front of it and lean back so the rolled mat sits across the mid-thoracic spine — roughly at the level of the shoulder blades. Extend the arms overhead or clasp the hands behind the head. Allow the thoracic spine to extend over the roll, opening the chest toward the ceiling. Breathe slowly and allow gravity to do the work. After one minute, shift the roll slightly higher toward the upper thoracic spine and hold for another minute.

This is one of the most effective thoracic mobility exercises available and directly counteracts the forward rounding that sitting produces. The client may hear or feel gentle clicking in the thoracic spine — this is normal and generally indicates the joints moving through a range they have not accessed recently.

### 6. Seated Wide-Leg Forward Fold — 2 minutes

Sit on the mat with both legs extended and spread as wide as comfortable. Flex both feet. Hinge forward from the hips — not the lower back — and walk the hands forward along the floor until a stretch is felt in the inner thighs and hamstrings. Hold for two full minutes, breathing into the restriction. Do not force the torso lower — allow gravity and breath to gradually deepen the position over the two minutes. This addresses adductor and hamstring tightness that limits squat depth and hip mobility.

### 7. Lat Stretch in Child's Pose — 90 seconds each side

From child's pose with arms extended forward, walk both hands to the right until the left side of the torso is fully lengthened. Place the right hand on top of the left to add gentle weight. Hold for ninety seconds, breathing into the left lat and side body. Switch sides. Lat tightness is a direct consequence of pull-up training and limits overhead reach — this stretch becomes increasingly important as pull-up volume increases through Phase 2 and Phase 3.

### 8. Neck and Upper Trapezius Release — 45 seconds each side

Sit cross-legged on the mat. Drop the right ear toward the right shoulder, allowing the weight of the head to create a gentle stretch through the left side of the neck and upper trapezius. Place the right hand lightly on top of the head — not pulling, just adding gentle weight. Hold for forty-five seconds. Switch sides. Upper trapezius tension is almost universal in people who use computers and phones and contributes to headaches, shoulder elevation during pull-ups, and general upper body tension.

### 9. Constructive Rest Position — 2 minutes

Lie on the back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart, arms resting by the sides with palms facing up. Close the eyes. Allow the lower back to settle naturally toward the floor — do not press it flat, just let it find its natural position. Breathe slowly and deliberately, allowing the body to become heavy. This position decompresses the lumbar spine, allows the hip flexors to fully release, and activates the parasympathetic nervous system in preparation for sleep.

During these two minutes, the client can practice a simple breathing protocol: inhale for four counts, hold for four counts, exhale for eight counts. The extended exhale activates the vagus nerve and accelerates the shift into parasympathetic dominance. This is not a mindfulness exercise — it is a physiological tool for improving recovery.

# Phase-Specific Mobility Emphases

## The Five Intensity Techniques (Phase 2 and 3)

**Mechanical Drop Sets:** Move from hardest to easiest variation within a movement pattern with no rest between variations. For pressing: Decline → Standard → Incline. For pulling: Chin-Up → Inverted Row horizontal → Inverted Row 45 degrees.

**Paused Reps:** Hold the most mechanically disadvantaged position for a prescribed count. Eliminates the stretch reflex and forces the muscle to generate force from a dead stop.

**Density Blocks:** Fixed time window, maximum quality reps. Progress by accumulating more reps in the same window each week.

**Rest-Pause Sets:** Perform to near-failure, rest fifteen seconds, continue, rest fifteen seconds, final cluster. All three clusters equal one set.

**Tempo Contrast:** Four-second eccentric, one-second pause, explosive concentric. Recruits both slow and fast-twitch fibres in the same set.

# The Complete 12-Week Home Strength Programme
### All Components Integrated — Final Master Document

---

# CLIENT PROFILE AND PROGRAMME OVERVIEW

**Client:** Male, 27 years old, beginner
**Training Location:** Small flat
**Equipment:** Yoga mat, doorway pull-up bar
**Programme Duration:** 12 weeks
**Sessions Per Week:** 3 strength sessions + 2–3 cardio sessions + 1 Saturday finisher + daily mobility work

---

## Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Training Focus | Cardio Focus | Saturday Theme |
|-------|-------|---------------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | 1–4 | Foundation and Motor Learning | LISS Base Building | Skill and Exploration |
| 2 | 5–8 | High Intensity Strength Development | LISS + MICT + HIIT | Competition and Challenge |
| 3 | 9–12 | Strength Consolidation and Performance | Performance Cardio | Performance and Celebration |

---

## The Six Movement Patterns

Every strength session trains most of these patterns. Progression within each pattern drives all strength development.

- **Horizontal Push** — press-up variations
- **Horizontal Pull** — inverted row variations
- **Vertical Pull** — pull-up and chin-up progressions
- **Squat** — bilateral and unilateral patterns
- **Hip Hinge** — glute bridge, single-leg hinge, Nordic curl
- **Core and Anti-Rotation** — plank, hollow body, dead bug

---

## The Five Intensity Techniques (Phase 2 and 3)

**Mechanical Drop Sets:** Move from hardest to easiest variation within a movement pattern with no rest between variations. For pressing: Decline → Standard → Incline. For pulling: Chin-Up → Inverted Row horizontal → Inverted Row 45 degrees.

**Paused Reps:** Hold the most mechanically disadvantaged position for a prescribed count. Eliminates the stretch reflex and forces the muscle to generate force from a dead stop.

**Density Blocks:** Fixed time window, maximum quality reps. Progress by accumulating more reps in the same window each week.

**Rest-Pause Sets:** Perform to near-failure, rest fifteen seconds, continue, rest fifteen seconds, final cluster. All three clusters equal one set.

**Tempo Contrast:** Four-second eccentric, one-second pause, explosive concentric. Recruits both slow and fast-twitch fibres in the same set.

---

## Nutrition Targets

**Calories:** Bodyweight in kg × 33–35 (training days), × 30–32 (rest days in Phase 1)
**Protein:** 1.8–2.2g per kg bodyweight daily, every day including rest days
**Carbohydrates:** 45–55% of total calories, higher on training days
**Fat:** 25–35% of total calories, minimum 0.8g per kg bodyweight
**Hydration:** 2.5–3 litres daily, 3–3.5 litres on training days

---

## The Three Mobility Routines

**Routine 1 — Morning Wake-Up (8–10 minutes):** Every morning upon waking. Supine knee hug, spinal twist, cat-cow, thread the needle, child's pose with lateral reach, hip flexor stretch, seated hamstring reach, ankle circles, thoracic extension, three deep breaths.

**Routine 2 — Pre-Session Primer (8–10 minutes):** Before every training session. Replaces all previously described warm-ups. Inchworm with press-up, world's greatest stretch, hip circle in deep squat, thoracic rotation in quadruped, leg swings, scapular wall slide, ankle dorsiflexion mobilisation, arm circle progression, jumping jacks.

**Routine 3 — Evening Wind-Down (12–15 minutes):** Three to four evenings per week on training days. Legs up the wall, figure-four hip stretch, couch stretch, doorframe chest stretch, thoracic extension over rolled mat, seated wide-leg forward fold, lat stretch in child's pose, neck and upper trapezius release, constructive rest position with breathing protocol.

---

## Supplement Protocol

**From Day 1:** Vitamin D3 1,000–2,000 IU daily. Protein powder as needed to hit targets.
**From Week 9:** Creatine monohydrate 3–5g daily.
**As needed:** Magnesium glycinate 200–400mg before bed. Fish oil 1–2g EPA/DHA daily. Zinc 15–25mg daily.
**Pre-training:** One cup of coffee 30–45 minutes before sessions.

---

# PHASE 1 — WEEKS 1–4
## Foundation and Motor Learning

**Training Goal:** Establish movement quality, build connective tissue resilience, develop body awareness, introduce training stress without overwhelming recovery.

**Tempo:** 3-1-1 on all exercises unless otherwise noted. Three seconds lowering, one second pause, one second lifting.

**Rest Periods:** 90 seconds between sets unless otherwise noted.

**Cardio:** Two LISS sessions per week on non-strength days.

**Mobility Emphasis:** Hip flexor release and thoracic spine activation. Add standalone hip flexor session on rest days. Add wrist preparation sequence to pre-session primer throughout Phase 1.

**Wrist Preparation Sequence (add to pre-session primer, Phase 1 only):** Ten slow wrist circles each direction. Backs of hands on floor, fingers toward knees, shift weight forward and back ten times. Prayer position hands lowered toward waist, hold twenty seconds.

---

## WEEK 1

### Strength Session A

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes** (as described in mobility section)

- Incline Press-Up (hands on windowsill or sturdy chair) — 3 × 10, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Dead Hang (overhand grip) — 3 × 20 seconds, 90 seconds rest
- Bodyweight Squat — 3 × 12, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Glute Bridge — 3 × 12, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Plank — 3 × 20 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- Scapular Pull-Up (depress and retract shoulder blades without bending elbows) — 3 × 8, 90 seconds rest

**Evening Wind-Down** recommended tonight.

---

### Strength Session B

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

- Incline Press-Up — 3 × 10, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Inverted Row (bar set low in doorframe, body at 45-degree angle, heels on floor) — 3 × 8, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Reverse Lunge — 3 × 8 each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 3 × 10 each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Dead Bug — 3 × 6 each side, controlled, 60 seconds rest
- Dead Hang — 3 × 25 seconds, 90 seconds rest

**Evening Wind-Down** recommended tonight.

---

### Strength Session C

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

- Incline Press-Up — 3 × 12, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Scapular Pull-Up — 3 × 10, 90 seconds rest
- Bodyweight Squat — 3 × 15, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Glute Bridge — 3 × 15, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Side Plank — 3 × 15 seconds each side, 60 seconds rest
- Inverted Row — 3 × 8, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest

**Evening Wind-Down** recommended tonight.

---

### Week 1 Cardio

**Cardio Session 1 — LISS Walk (20 minutes)**
Walking in place with high knees for twenty continuous minutes. Divide into four five-minute blocks. Block one: relaxed arms. Block two: nasal breathing focus. Block three: higher knee drive. Block four: relaxed shoulders. Play music or a podcast.

**Cardio Session 2 — LISS Shadow Boxing (20 minutes)**
Move continuously around the mat space for twenty minutes throwing light punches and shifting weight foot to foot. Four five-minute rounds with thirty seconds rest between rounds.

---

### Week 1 Saturday — The Deck of Cards

**Warm-Up — 5 minutes** (standard Saturday warm-up)
Jumping jacks 30 seconds, hip circles 10 each direction, arm circles 10 each direction, leg swings 10 each leg front-back, leg swings 10 each leg side-side, slow bodyweight squats 8 reps, inchworm 5 reps, thoracic rotation 8 each side, three deep breaths.

**Main Event — 20 minutes**
Assign suits to exercises: Hearts = Press-Up, Diamonds = Bodyweight Squat, Clubs = Glute Bridge, Spades = Mountain Climber (each knee drive = one rep). Shuffle deck. Flip cards one at a time. Number on card = reps. Face cards = 10 reps. Aces = 11 reps. Jokers = 30 seconds maximum effort of any exercise. Get through as many cards as possible in twenty minutes. Record number of cards completed.

**Cool-Down — 5 minutes** (standard Saturday cool-down)
Walk in place slowing gradually 60 seconds, standing quad stretch 20 seconds each leg, standing hip flexor stretch 20 seconds each leg, doorframe chest stretch 30 seconds, seated hamstring stretch 30 seconds each leg, child's pose 30 seconds, three deep breaths.

---

## WEEK 2

### Strength Session A

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

- Incline Press-Up — 3 × 12, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Dead Hang — 3 × 30 seconds, 90 seconds rest
- Bodyweight Squat — 3 × 15, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Glute Bridge — 3 × 15, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Plank — 3 × 25 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- Scapular Pull-Up — 3 × 10, 90 seconds rest

---

### Strength Session B

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

- Incline Press-Up — 3 × 12, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Inverted Row — 3 × 10, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Reverse Lunge — 3 × 10 each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 3 × 12 each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 each side, 60 seconds rest
- Dead Hang — 3 × 30 seconds, 90 seconds rest

---

### Strength Session C

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

- Floor Press-Up (introduce if incline feels controlled, otherwise continue incline at 3 × 15) — 3 × 8, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Scapular Pull-Up — 3 × 12, 90 seconds rest
- Bodyweight Squat — 3 × 15, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 3 × 12 each leg, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest
- Side Plank — 3 × 20 seconds each side, 60 seconds rest
- Inverted Row — 3 × 10, 3-1-1 tempo, 90 seconds rest

---

### Week 2 Cardio

**Cardio Session 1 — LISS Walk (25 minutes)**
As week one but five minutes longer. Same four-block structure.

**Cardio Session 2 — LISS Mobility Flow (25 minutes)**
Move continuously through the following sequence for 25 minutes without stopping. Cat-cow 8 reps, child's pose 20 seconds, downward dog 20 seconds, hip flexor stretch right 20 seconds, hip flexor stretch left 20 seconds, seated hamstring stretch 20 seconds, thoracic rotation right 10 seconds, thoracic rotation left 10 seconds. Repeat continuously.

---

### Week 2 Saturday — The Ladder Challenge

**Warm-Up — 5 minutes**

**Main Event — 20–25 minutes**
Climb from one rep to ten reps and back down to one. Exercises per round: Press-Up, Bodyweight Squat, Dead Bug each side. Round 1: 1 of each. Round 2: 2 of each. Continue to Round 10: 10 of each. Then descend: Round 11: 9 of each, continuing back to Round 20: 1 of each. Rest as needed between rounds but keep rest short. Record total time to complete the full ladder.

**Cool-Down — 5 minutes**

---

## WEEK 3

### Strength Session A

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

## High Intensity Strength Development

**Training Goal:** Build genuine strength through progressive overload, introduce intensity techniques, develop pulling strength toward unassisted pull-ups.

**Training Structure:** Upper/Lower split across three sessions per week. Rotation: Upper A, Lower A, Upper B in week one of cycle. Lower B, Upper A, Lower A in week two.

**Tempo:** 2-1-1 for most exercises. Specific exceptions noted per session.

**Rest Periods:** Precisely prescribed per session. Rest periods are part of the intensity prescription.

**Session Length:** 55–70 minutes.

**Cardio:** Two to three sessions per week. One LISS (30–35 minutes), one MICT (20–25 minutes), one HIIT (15–20 minutes, introduced week six).

**Mobility Emphasis:** Shoulder external rotation and thoracic extension. Add shoulder external rotation work to evening wind-down. Perform doorframe chest stretch twice daily.

**Nutrition Adjustment:** Push toward upper end of calorie target (bodyweight × 35). Introduce meal timing — eat two to three hours before training, protein-rich meal within two hours post-training, pre-sleep casein protein (200g cottage cheese or Greek yoghurt).

### Upper A — Pull Focus with Rest-Pause Introduction

**Pre-Session Primer — 8 minutes**

**Primary Strength Block — Vertical Pull**

*Chin-Up or Negative Chin-Up — Rest-Pause Sets*
Three rest-pause sets. For each: perform as many full chin-ups as possible (or negatives with 5-second lower if full reps unavailable), rest exactly 15 seconds, perform more reps, rest exactly 15 seconds, perform final cluster. Record total reps across all three clusters for each rest-pause set. This is the benchmark to beat next week. Rest 3 minutes between rest-pause sets.

**Secondary Strength Block — Horizontal Pull**

*Inverted Row — Mechanical Drop Set*
Set bar as low as possible so body is nearly horizontal. Perform as many rows as possible with body horizontal, immediately transition to 45-degree body angle and continue, immediately transition to 60-degree body angle and continue. That is one mechanical drop set. Three mechanical drop sets, 90 seconds rest between each. Aim for 6–8 reps horizontal, 4–6 at 45 degrees, 4–6 at 60 degrees.

**Tertiary Block — Horizontal Push**

*Press-Up — Tempo Contrast*
Four sets of 8 reps. Lower for 4 seconds, pause 1 second at bottom, drive up as explosively as possible. 75 seconds rest between sets.
